Even if he fails, he’ll have done more than the people waiting for a safe moment to jump ship. Americans have more in common than Washington gives them credit for. articles.title: Flaw in Linux NFS file sharing exposes servers to remote takeover
articles.content:
The vulnerability went undetected in the Linux kernel for 12 years and allows anyone who reaches a server's file-sharing port to gain root access without a password.

Researchers have found a critical flaw in the Linux kernel’s NFS file-sharing server that lets unauthenticated attackers obtain a root shell on affected systems. The flaw remained undetected in the kernel for 12 years, until two researchers, one using an AI agent, discovered it independently.

NFS is typically used inside local networks, including in container networks in Kubernetes clusters and on build servers in development environments. However, it is also enabled on many embedded devices and in network-attached storage (NAS) devices which might be running older kernel versions and can only be patched with firmware updates.

Tracked as CVE-2026-99362 and dubbed NFS2ROOT, the flaw affects systems running the NFSv4.1 or NFSv4.2 versions of the Network File System protocol, the default in many Linux distributions. The vulnerability allows anyone who can reach a server’s port 2049 to corrupt the memory of the nfsd process, the kernel component that serves NFS requests. It is rated 9.8 in severity.

A researcher with French security agency ANSSI, Jérémy Jean, found the bug in August, and his fix was merged into the mainline kernel on September 14.

According to security firm OpenSec Intelligence, which also discovered the heap overflow vulnerability and published technical details about it this week, the flaw can be exploited to gain a shell with root privileges. OpenSec found the bug using its AI-powered security testing harness and submitted its own patch to the Linux kernel maintainers on September 22.

However, since it takes time for all supported kernel branches to backport fixes, the bug wasn’t disclosed, nor was a CVE ID assigned, until November 19.

The flaw was introduced in Linux 3.16 in 2014 and is now patched in eight stable kernel branches: 5.10.275, 5.15.226, 6.1.193, 6.6.163, 6.12.117, 6.18.61, 7.3.2 and 7.4-rc1.

On systems that can’t be immediately patched, administrators are advised to use firewall rules that block access to port 2049 from untrusted systems. Another option is to turn off NFSv4.1 and 4.2 in the nfsd config and then restart the service, but this will turn off pNFS and some features.

A president can pick up the phone without taking over a company. That distinction is getting lost in the uproar over Nvidia. Donald Trump was right to urge the board to bring back its chief executive. A company at the center of America’s chip industry had good reason to think twice before letting its most valuable talent walk out the door.

The headlines want us to dwell on allegations about the CEO’s private life. I don’t care who he was seeing. If there was a national security breach, that’s a different matter. Speculation about espionage doesn’t establish one. The board still had to make a business decision, and ordinary Americans with retirement savings had a stake in how it turned out. Why should Nvidia hand a rival the chance to hire the person who helped build the company?

Think back to the financial crisis. Barack Obama’s administration pushed out the head of General Motors as part of its rescue of the automaker. Trump urging a board to reconsider its decision is a far cry from Washington using bailout money to reshape a company’s leadership. Lawmakers are free to ask questions. Turning a phone call into grounds for impeachment would be a stretch, and hauling directors before Congress to intimidate them would be an abuse of oversight.

What worries me most is the opening this gives politicians who want more control over artificial intelligence. We’ve already seen Washington lean on social media companies over what people could say online. Now imagine that kind of pressure applied to the tools people use to search, write, and work.

Trump was right to speak up for keeping that expertise on America’s team. Nvidia’s board had a job to do. It didn’t need Congress looking over its shoulder, and Washington doesn’t need an excuse to run the AI industry.

articles.title: The Pilgrims and the opportunity of crisis
articles.content:
Podcast: Play in new window | Download | Embed

Subscribe: Apple Podcasts | RSS

Once the Pilgrims landed at Plymouth Rock, they soon realized they were outmatched by nature and the New England elements. Half of their company did not make it through the first winter, yet the Pilgrims persevered. When spring came, and the Mayflower prepared to make the journey back to England, not a single Pilgrim was on board. They chose to pursue their dreams of living in a land of civil and religious liberty.

Much to their surprise, a solitary Indian called Samoset emerged from the woods. He spoke broken English, which he had learned from English explorers and fishermen who had visited the coast. Samoset told them about the history of the land where they had established their settlement.

A fierce war tribe known as the Patauxet once lived there. However, a plague swept through their village and killed every last one of them. The other tribes in the area believed the Great Spirit had wiped out the Patauxet because of their bloodlust. The other tribes would not set foot on the land, leaving it abandoned and available for the Pilgrims when they arrived.

The Pilgrims learned much from Samoset, and they considered him a friend. When he departed, he promised to return and bring others with him. True to his word, Samoset returned with Chief Massasoit and several warriors. Among the warriors was an Indian named Squanto. He spoke perfect English, which amazed the Pilgrims.

How was it that an Indian in the New World understood and spoke perfect, unbroken English?

Squanto’s backstory is fascinating and enjoyable to study. Six years before the Pilgrims’ arrival, in 1614, an English captain named Thomas Hunt was exploring the coast. Hunt and his men kidnapped 27 Indians, one of whom was Squanto. They took the captives to Spain with the plan of selling them into slavery.

Catholic priests and friars in Spain learned of Hunt’s plan to sell the Indians, so they purchased them and set them free. Squanto worked his way to England, where he lived for five years. He learned the language and immersed himself in the English culture.

He returned back to the New World in 1619 with another English captain named Thomas Dermer. When Squanto arrived, he discovered his entire tribe had been wiped out by the plague. He joined the Wampanoag tribe, who took him in as a brother.

Squanto was in the perfect position to help the Pilgrims. He understood the English language perfectly. He understood the English culture and could predict how the Pilgrims would attempt to survive in their new location, but he also understood the land of New England. He had the skills needed to hunt, fish, raise crops, and survive the harsh elements of the New World.

Squanto took it upon himself to adopt the Pilgrims and teach them what they needed to learn in order to sustain themselves as a thriving community.

That first Thanksgiving feast was shared by the Pilgrims with Squanto, Chief Massasoit, and 90 of his warriors. For three days they played games together, feasted together, and developed friendships which lasted for years.

William Bradford said Squanto “was a special instrument sent of God for (our) good.” Squanto was a colonial version of Joseph. Joseph was sold into slavery by his own brothers. When Joseph confronted his brothers years later, he stated: “As for you, you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good, to bring it about that many people should be kept alive, as they are today” (Gen. 50:20).

What Thomas Hunt and his men meant for evil against Squanto, God was able to turn it to good to bring it about that the Pilgrims should be kept alive during their early years. Since the very foundation and Biblical roots of American values can be traced back to the Pilgrims, we owe Squanto a great debt of gratitude.

Watching the Hand of Providence unfold throughout America’s history is a beautiful thing to behold.

Because of God’s protection, the Pilgrims’ perseverance, and their strong desire to pursue religious and civil liberties, we now have the opportunity to live in the strongest and freest country known to history.

Now you know the full story. Share it, especially with young people. They must know the truth of our heritage and the guiding Hand of Providence which has shaped America since its beginning.

Before we teach children to think of Thanksgiving as a day of mourning, we ought to tell them about Squanto. The Pilgrims lost roughly half their company in their first winter. When the Mayflower sailed back to England, the survivors stayed. They had come seeking civil and religious liberty. It took a man who had every reason to distrust the English to help them survive.

In 1614, an English captain named Thomas Hunt seized Squanto and took him to Spain to sell him into slavery. Catholic friars intervened. Squanto made his way to England, where he learned the language. When he finally returned home, he discovered that an epidemic had devastated his people. He knew the land where the Pilgrims settled because it had been his home. He showed them how to fish and raise crops.

I see the hand of Providence in that choice. In Genesis, Joseph tells the brothers who sold him into slavery that God turned their evil intent to good and kept many people alive. Hunt’s cruelty was still cruelty. It did not have the last word. Squanto helped keep a struggling community alive. At the harvest feast, the Pilgrims shared three days of food and fellowship with Chief Massasoit and his men.

That fellowship did not last forever. Children should learn about the wars and wrongs that followed as they grow old enough to understand them. But when Loudoun County makes materials about the National Day of Mourning available to elementary teachers, parents are right to ask whether their children are also hearing what made that harvest worth celebrating.

We should teach children why those neighbors sat down to eat together. Then we should sit down at our own tables and give thanks for the people whose generosity has made our lives possible. That is what Thanksgiving is for.

Well, happy Thanksgiving, everybody. One and all. I I trust that. Well, I don’t know.

Maybe you’ve already eaten. I was about to say, I trust that you’re going to enjoy a delicious Thanksgiving dinner, but I don’t know. It’s possible that you eat early. I don’t know.

Maybe, maybe you’re full. Maybe you’re maybe you’re already nestled in and on the couch and watching football. I don’t know why you’d be listening to me while watching football. Unless you’ve got the TV muted, that’s a possibility.

You might just have it muted and you might have me on. I don’t know. Regardless. Happy Thanksgiving, everyone.

And well, we’re here. And we’re in the middle, really, every Thanksgiving this entire week. We throw ourselves into history class and we’re there today. We’re in the middle of history class.

And we’ve approached history class a little differently this week that we have in the past. A lot of times we just we start with a particular date and we we highlight the the history of it. But this year I think we’ve we’ve started with some themes and we’ve highlighted the the history around those themes. On Monday, we we dealt with the Mayflower Compact and really what the Mayflower Compact has given us.

And that led us into Tuesday. Wednesday, we we spent some time talking, I guess what what we normally do. We talked a little bit about history. We talked about the the event of of the Mayflower crossing the Atlantic, but but really we we did.

We landed on a theme. And and the theme is or was from yesterday. Sometimes crises present opportunities. We have to keep our eyes open to those opportunities.

And I don’t know, I think maybe that theme might carry over into today. The story of the pilgrim’s journey leading up to and crossing the Atlantic, it’s a miraculous one, truly it is. And and as we talked about yesterday, a lot of times you can look back and you can see the golden thread of providence woven throughout the entire expedition. And we we can see that even in our own lives.

If if we take the time to look back, we can we can pause. We can see the the the golden thread of of of Providence. articles.title: COP31 and the unraveling of the global climate agenda
articles.content:
There is no authoritative total-cost figure for the UN’s COP31 climate conference in the luxury resort city of Antalya, Turkey, covering all countries, organizations, NGOs, businesses, and participants combined. However, we do know that COP31 reportedly had about 93,000 registered in-person participants (plus several thousand virtual attendees). Research on the official booking platform found a median accommodation cost of roughly €2,420, or about US$2,780 for the conference period, with properties near the venue averaging more.

And then there is airfare to Turkey from the over 190 countries that sent representatives, and ground transportation for them all each day as well. Taken together, delegates easily spent an amount approaching one half billion dollars just to get to the conference and stay in local accommodation.

But that is just the tip of the billion-dollar COP31 iceberg. If tens of thousands of government officials, NGO staff, journalists, lobbyists and corporate representatives spent two weeks at COP31, the salaries paid while they were traveling and attending almost certainly exceeded the travel bill itself. And what about:

  • meals,
  • conference facilities,
  • security,
  • exhibition booths,
  • interpreters,
  • NGO and corporate events,
  • media operations,
  • host-government expenditures.

It would not be surprising if the true worldwide resource cost of COP31 was measured in billions rather than hundreds of millions of dollars…for a conference about a non-existent problem that failed to even remotely achieve what its supporters had hoped for. Thankfully, only a few million dollars were wasted sending American representatives to the COP flop since the Trump administration has wisely pulled out of the entire ridiculous process.

Regardless, COP31 trundled on and may have been the world’s largest gathering of world leaders and decision-makers to address the so-called climate crisis. But there was little to show for it. The conference was scheduled to conclude on November 20, but due to delayed negotiations, it ran over into the weekend (see the graph below of the record-breaking overtime). Nevertheless, agreements were slow in coming, and there was no overarching treaty to limit the use of fossil fuels. For the climate zealots, this spells disaster for our planet. But for climate realists, those of us who recognize that climate change is mostly natural and humanity’s contribution is essentially negligible, this is a great relief.

COP31 had the longest overtime out of all previous COP conferences

Although most participant countries were quick to agree that humans are causing a climate crisis due to our emissions from coal, oil, and natural gas, fossil fuels weren’t even mentioned in the draft of the final agreement. In truth, no country wants to impoverish its citizens by limiting its abundant and reliable energy sources, and so although they are quick to pay lip service to working together to avert catastrophe, when it gets down to the brass tacks, few want to be locked into binding climate agreements.

What started out as enthusiastic pledges to save the world dwindled to what Rachel Cleetus of the Union of Concerned Scientists called “a bleak overtime, with dwindling food and water, and no sign of any progress since the alarmingly underwhelming texts we saw earlier.”

So the conference ended without any significant, solid political agreement, with member countries rejecting the final draft, which did not include fossil fuel restrictions. The EU representative said that “We will not endorse a cover decision, or an Antalya pact, that does not even mention fossil fuels, which is the key driver of climate change.” Moreover, with the United States not attending as a member country, other nations were reluctant to make binding agreements. The draft agreement focused on industrial Carbon Capture, Utilization and Storage (CCUS) targets of at least 500 million metric tons of carbon dioxide per year by 2035, with the goal of 1.3 to 2.5 gigatons annually. Additionally, they introduced the goal for so-called clean electricity to supply 35% of the world’s energy by 2035, though this was only supported by 90 out of the 196 participating countries. Turkey’s COP31 president, Murat Kurum, lamented, “There is nothing to do; we did all that we could. Since there are 196 countries, they will make the decision, and we will respect their decision.”

Many countries are still pursuing net zero, but a worldwide agreement for stricter targets never materialized. Some nations have formed smaller alliances to push for faster emission cuts and initiate financial programs. Some groups include the Conference on Transitioning Away from Fossil Fuels (TAFF), the Green Grids ​Initiative, the Global Methane Pledge, and ⁠the Beyond Oil and Gas Alliance. The TAFF, for instance, is planning a conference next year with representatives from roughly ninety countries, including Britain, Mexico and Nigeria.

Despite these smaller initiatives, the lack of an overarching agreement is promising: the climate scare is dying, even if it has been slow in coming. Without mention of fossil fuel reduction in the final COP31 draft, many are saying that they didn’t address the primary cause for concern. Indeed, Saudi Arabia and Russia were against mentioning fossil fuels in any agreement. Commitments to give funds to vulnerable countries have been removed from agreements. At the climate summit, Panama’s environment minister, Juan Carlos Navarro, said that “We are being held hostage by the petroleum mafia.” Other developing countries and island states have shared similar sentiments, claiming that they are struggling the most with climate change.

Yet those promoting common sense policies should be relieved that the “petroleum mafia” is, in fact, getting its way. After all, it is through fossil fuel usage that developing countries can alleviate poverty and ensure resiliency against natural disasters and natural changes in climate. So why, year after year, are we wasting billions of dollars sending delegates around the world in this charade of saving the planet? This year’s attendance skyrocketed compared to past years, with over 95,000 participants, as seen in the graph below from Carbon Brief.

Attendance at COP31 compared to previous years

Hopefully next year, we will see a decline in this charade as countries grapple with real-world economic and social issues. The climate change crusade is still the politically correct position in much of the world, of course, but with world leaders failing to make binding commitments, we can’t expect the public to continue to take it seriously for much longer. The scare will die: let’s do what we can to accelerate its demise!

Affects Drupal core before 10.6.23, 11.3.23 or 11.4.14 on sites in an unusual or incomplete install state with an unsecured installer. Fixed in 10.6.23, 11.3.23 and 11.4.14.

Drupal core has an access bypass flaw that lets an attacker take over the site, reaching it remotely without logging in. It needs a non-default setup in which the site's installer is left remotely accessible and the site is in an unusual or incomplete install state, and it is listed as exploited in attacks by CISA.

Written by a model

Teams running Drupal core 10.6.x, 11.3.x or 11.4.x sites whose install.php installer is not secured, especially sites in an unusual or incomplete install state, including production.

articles.title: Leaked EU Draft Would Allow Mass Scanning of Private Messages
articles.content:
If you're tired of censorship and surveillance, subscribe to Reclaim The Net.

Leaked documents have revealed that a secret, unpublished draft deal on the EU’s Child Sexual Abuse Regulation, dubbed Chat Control 2.0, contains a provision that would allow an “independent administrative authority” (i.e., not a court) to order mass scanning of private messages of all users for up to 24 months at a time, as well as force providers to scan specific parts of their service.

Another revelation is that the Irish Council Presidency, with the Commission’s backing, has been trying to bypass Parliament’s negotiators who have refused to accept this, and instead take the proposal to the group leaders.

This is happening in the context of the trilogue negotiations on Chat Control 2.0, where the seventh, and possibly final, meeting is scheduled for December 8. EU ambassadors (COREPER) are set to meet on December 2.

The document in question is a Council one, numbered WK 16725 2026 INIT, and was drafted by the Parliament’s rapporteur, Javier Zarzalejos (EPP, Spain), and the Irish Presidency. It was made public by Patrick Breyer, a digital rights advocate, who said that the deal breaks both the Council’s and the Parliament’s negotiating mandates by introducing indiscriminate, mandatory mass surveillance of private communications.

According to Breyer, this “independent administrative authority” would be able to issue “detection orders” for the scanning of private messages of all users, with the only limit being that it would have to be for a limited period of 24 months at a time.

This means that European email and chat providers that do not scan today would be forced to do so, while US-based ones would have to use “error-prone AI algorithms to analyze private text chats and ‘unknown’ visuals.”

The “independent administrative authority” would be able to act on its own, without a court order, and issue detection orders whenever a part of the provider’s service has been used for the purpose of child sexual abuse.

The orders could cover “a specific part of the provider’s service, or channel, functionality or other category of communication of that service.” Breyer notes that the scanning of “parts of a service” or “functionalities” is in reality scanning every private message of millions of innocent citizens without individual suspicion, and adds, “In the real world, this would translate to police searching ‘the functionality of envelopes’ to open all letters. It is a semantic trick to rebrand mass surveillance.”

The document’s wording on encryption is such that it excludes “weakening or undermining end-to-end encryption” and “decrypting data” – but it does not rule out client-side scanning, i.e., scanning of messages on the phone before encryption. This means that WhatsApp, which is end-to-end encrypted, could be forced to build this type of scanning into its app.

The Commission’s own impact assessment from 2022 found that detection orders would lead to a 354% increase in reported communications, both true and false. The document also seeks to make “Chat Control 1.0” – voluntary scanning – permanent.

Meanwhile, the Parliament’s position, adopted in November 2023 with a near-unanimous vote, is that scanning should only be allowed of specific suspects and with a judicial warrant, while encryption must be protected and client-side scanning rejected.

All of the Parliament’s negotiators, except for the EPP, refused to sign the text, which prompted the Commission to label them as “extremely intransigent” and call for “unusually robust means and positions” from the Council.

The German Permanent Representation in the EU sent a cable on November 18 to Berlin that was published by Contexte and obtained by heise online. The cable refers to a November 13 meeting of the Council’s working group and reveals that the Irish Presidency would, if necessary, move the negotiations to the political group leaders in the Parliament, bypassing the negotiators.

However, the website heise.de reports that, according to Contexte, this meeting has not taken place, while Dublin has denied holding such contacts with the group leaders. Digital Society’s Konstantin Macher said the attempt to bypass the Parliament’s negotiators was “scandalous.”

At this point, the EU Council can still block the proposal if a group of countries representing 35% of the bloc’s population do so in the COREPER meeting on December 2.

Comments from Italy, Poland, Bulgaria, and Greece have been critical of the latest proposal, while Finland, the Netherlands, Croatia, Cyprus, and Austria have submitted formal scrutiny reservations.

Germany, which in the past said that “private communication must never be under general suspicion” and that “Germany will not agree to such proposals at EU level,” has not followed through on its own words, Breyer said. Instead, Germany “has so far failed to reject mandatory scanning orders in the negotiations and does not even require limiting them to specific suspects.”

According to heise.de, Berlin is prepared to show flexibility on the issue of mandatory orders only if the full scope of “voluntary” scanning is kept in the final version of the proposal.

This is happening despite the fact that the error rate of automated scanning is high, and false alarms frequent. Breyer noted that the EU Commission’s own evaluation shows that providers report error rates of up to 20%, while police data confirms that up to 75% of flagged chats are false alarms.

In Germany, the BKA (Federal Criminal Police Office) reported in 2024 that 48.3% of the 205,728 reports received from the US-based National Center for Missing and Exploited Children (NCMEC) were not criminally relevant.

We have previously covered the 2023 Legal Service opinion, according to which the snooping plans interfere with fundamental rights; Germany’s 48% error-rate report, and the EU’s push to make scanning permanent despite the high error rate; the reports that Chat Control reports are processed with the help of Palantir software; and the Council advancing its scanning proposal in September.

The Council’s own Legal Service warned in 2023 that the proposed detection orders could be struck down by the EU Court of Justice as general and indiscriminate surveillance. And yet – the Irish Presidency is trying to push through a deal that would allow for precisely that.

articles.title: New York "Age Verification" Law Faces First Amendment Challenge
articles.content:
If you're tired of censorship and surveillance, subscribe to Reclaim The Net.

NetChoice is going to court once again to stop New York state from enforcing another controversial law, this one requiring platforms to check everyone's age, in order to continue showing New Yorkers the feeds they already use.

"New York cannot tell social media companies how to organize the speech on their services any more than it can tell the New York Times how to order the articles displayed in its paper," says Paul Taske, NetChoice Litigation Center.

The organization's argument is that the law, known as the SAFE for Kids Act, affects not only children, but all users, including adults, who will be forced to have their age verified in order to see a "personalized organization of lawful speech."

As NetChoice sees it, New York cannot make every New Yorker prove their age just to see a personalized organization of lawful speech.

The law was challenged in a filing in the US District Court, Southern District of New York, on November 23, as NetChoice v. James. The filing is a complaint for declaratory and injunctive relief, against Attorney General Letitia James.

The law takes effect on January 25, 2027, while the attorney general's rules, to which the complaint refers, were finalized on July 28, 2026.

The law states that platforms must use "commercially reasonable and technically feasible methods to determine that the covered user is not a covered minor" before showing anyone a personalized feed.

This means that "covered websites" must "verify the ages of all users to display personalized feeds even to adults," the complaint says. The alternative is to obtain "verifiable parental consent" for minors, which means parents will have to verify their own age as well.

The upshot is that adults will be forced to undergo age verification or risk ceding anonymity, the filing continues. And that opens up a whole other can of worms, as "adults may wish to explore political, religious, medical, or other sensitive subjects without linking their identities to those interests."

NetChoice is worried that checking every user's age "requires collecting sensitive data, such as government IDs, face scans, or behavioral data that third parties use to estimate age, and every database is a new target for breaches."

The rules proposed by the attorney general allow for "age estimation, age inference, or age verification," while verification can be done using "government-provided identification."

New York's own cost analysis, according to the complaint, shows that the rules "may deter 25% of users who reach the age-determination appeals process from completing that process."

While the rules are clear in many of their demands, they are also vague in some, such as whether the anti-circumvention duty "extends to preventing users from employing virtual private networks."

The SAFE for Kids Act bans personalized feeds for users under 18 without parental consent, and also bans notifications about feeds to minors "between the hours of 12 AM Eastern and 6 AM Eastern" without consent. The attorney general enforces the law, with "civil penalties up to $5,000 per violation."

The complaint names some of the NetChoice members affected by the law: Tumblr, YouTube, Facebook, Instagram, Threads, Pinterest, Reddit, X, and TikTok.

The legal arguments presented in the filing are that the law violates the First and Fourteenth Amendments, while also being preempted by Section 230.

As Taske put it, "Speech curation and presentation decisions are protected by the First Amendment, and the SAFE for Kids Act unconstitutionally interferes with them."

The complaint cites the 2024 case Moody v. NetChoice, which established that platforms decide what to "include and exclude, organize and prioritize."

The filing also refers to the Section 230 preemption, saying that the law is therefore preempted "because its requirements would force regulated websites to fundamentally change how they publish user-generated content or face punishing liability."

The complaint argues that "acts of arranging and sorting content are integral to the function of publishing."

NetChoice also notes that courts have already blocked similar laws in Arkansas, Utah, and Louisiana.

The organization adds that parents already have tools to control what their children can and cannot see online, and that the Act merely makes them make those decisions "through State-approved channels, when and how the State dictates."

This is the second lawsuit NetChoice has filed in New York this month, as on November 13 it challenged S.4505, which would make social media companies show state warning labels to users in New York under 17, repeatedly.

NetChoice views both laws as showing that "New York wants to control what speech websites present to New Yorkers, replacing the preferences of users and families with the state's."

As for the SAFE for Kids Act, the case is now in the hands of the US District Court, Southern District of New York, while NetChoice has asked for declarations and an injunction.

This is not the first time we have covered various attempts to impose age verification in the US - and specifically in New York.

We covered NetChoice's previous challenge to another New York law, S.4505, which would have social media companies show state warning labels to users in New York under 17, repeatedly.

We wrote about New York's law that requires adults to verify their age before using a chatbot, and a New York bill that would force age verification checks at the device level.

The SAFE for Kids Act is another example of how a law that starts with the goal of protecting children ends up affecting every adult in a given jurisdiction. In this case, it means that in order to be allowed to see a feed that an algorithm has picked for them, people will have to prove their age to the platform.

This can be done by handing over ID, undergoing a face scan, or allowing the platform to profile them based on their data. And that last option means giving up any possibility of reading the web anonymously.

articles.title: Virginia and Oregon Coordinate Grok Lawsuits Built on a Very Broad Definition of Harm
articles.content:
If you're tired of censorship and surveillance, subscribe to Reclaim The Net.

Two US states, Virginia and Oregon, have separately sued the maker of an AI image generation tool, but coordinated the lawsuits announced on the same day, and clearly working off the same playbook, including some dubious interpretations of what constitutes an offense.

The real and very serious problem of child sexual abuse material (CSAM) and non-consensual intimate images is not only often used as a battering ram against online platforms and tech companies, but also mixed in with other, much more spurious claims, that often amount to censorship and speech suppression.

Virginia AG Jay Jones and Oregon AG Dan Rayfield are targeting X, its parent company, and CEO Elon Musk’s SpaceX, and the lawsuits deal with safeguards – or lack thereof – against CSAM, non-consensual intimate images, and “other non-consensual sexualized images.”

Jones said in a statement that the lawsuit is “about seeking justice for the millions of Virginians who maintain accounts on X and were misled by the company’s false reassurances that their data and images would be safe on the platform.”

While CSAM and non-consensual intimate images are clearly defined as illegal and abusive, and nobody defends them, the logic of blaming a platform and its tools for this content, created and uploaded by users, would create new precedent. It’s akin to blaming Adobe for what somebody made in Photoshop and could have profound implications on being able to sue platforms for the alleged “harm” created by users.

Both complaints define “non-consensual sexualized images” to include people “in revealing clothing such as bikinis or underwear.”

The suits then proceed to count as evidence of X’s alleged wrongdoing the fact Grok, the AI tool, put people in bikinis, and sometimes as a joke – including Musk sharing an image of himself in a bikini, and another of a toaster in a bikini, with the comment, “Not sure why, but I couldn’t stop laughing about this one.”

Virginia’s own test account, meanwhile, got Grok to produce “an image of a real person with enhanced muscles and smaller, tighter clothing” after a reworded prompt – and the complaint counts this as a moderation failure.

In fact, Virginia says that Grok should have asked the user if they had the person’s consent to use or modify their photo. This would mean that the tool has to check every image of a real person, and verify the identity of every user, to make sure they have the necessary consent.

The Center for Countering Digital Harm (CCDH) has a January study that is cited in both complaints, and press releases announcing them. CCDH at the time said that Grok produced 3 million generally “sexualized” images in just 11 days.

The group’s definition of a “sexualized” image is extremely broad: it can include “a person in underwear, swimwear or similarly revealing clothing.”

CCDH said it used “an AI tool to identify the proportion of these images that are sexualized” – and also admitted that its findings “do not provide an assessment of how many of the images were created without the consent of the people pictured.”

The study is a major part of the evidence cited in the complaints, but it’s not the only one. Virginia alleges that xAI sent more than 135,000 reports to the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children (NCMEC) from September to December 2025, and “more than 90% of those reports were initially deemed inactionable.”

Grok is also said to have “explained which kinds of words triggered its filters.”

As for the relief the two states are seeking, Virginia wants an injunction, restitution, disgorgement, and civil penalties of up to $2,500 per violation for each willful violation. Oregon also wants an injunction and disgorgement, as well as civil penalties to be determined at trial, and a jury trial.

This is not the first time that states have gone after X and its tools, and not the first time that the legal efforts have been based on highly questionable interpretations of what is harmful and illegal, and what is not.

The theory of the lawsuit – that the design of a product makes its maker liable for the way the product is used – has been tried before. We recently covered a “nudification law” in Minnesota that targets the software rather than those making or sharing the images. xAI sued, and the Eighth Circuit has blocked the law as applied to xAI pending appeal.

The law, said xAI, captures “benign images of people in shorts (inner thigh), men without shirts (breast), and competitive swimmers (buttocks and breast).”

That law, xAI said, “lacks any exception for images with genuine artistic, satirical, journalistic, scientific, educational, medical, religious, or (most troublingly) political value.”

In January, seven Democratic senators asked several platforms to take action against “non-nude” images that are created using generative AI tools, and are sexualized, including “bikini” and “non-nude” images of individuals without their consent.

articles.title: Indiana Sued Over Law That Would Card Adults Every 100 Hours Online
articles.content:
If you're tired of censorship and surveillance, subscribe to Reclaim The Net.

The never-ending story of US state laws attempting to force platforms to check and recheck their users’ age continues, and so does the effort to fight those in court.

On November 18, NetChoice sued the state of Indiana in a federal court, asking it to declare the social media-related parts of HEA 1408 as unconstitutional under the First Amendment, and block them with preliminary and permanent injunctions.

We obtained a copy of the lawsuit for you here.

These parts of the law are set to come into force on January 1, 2027, and the defendant is Attorney General Todd Rokita, in his official capacity. The case is NetChoice v. Rokita, and it was filed in the US District Court for the Southern District of Indiana (Indianapolis).

The law in question says that social media platforms must “use commercially reasonable means, such as a neutral age screen mechanism, to determine the age and state of residence of the individual requesting creation of the account.”

An “adolescent” is defined as anyone under 16, who can only open an account with verifiable parental consent.

The privacy implications of this do not end there, nor do they only concern children. In fact, the law applies to all new account holders in Indiana, regardless of age. As NetChoice, a trade association representing the tech industry, puts it, “Every Hoosier gets carded, not just kids.”

The law ends up “burdening adult social media users by requiring that they repeatedly provide identification to verify their age,” the complaint states.

NetChoice Litigation Center Director Paul Taske said, “But Indiana’s HEA 1408 conditions both teen and adult access to social media on complying with state-mandated digital ID requirements.”

The filing continues, “By forcing adults to either surrender sensitive personal information (in this case, repeatedly for up to ten years) to access protected speech or drastically curtail their consumption of protected speech,” the law violates the Constitution.

As for the age checks, they keep coming back: within 14 days of 25 hours in a six-month period; again at 50 hours; then after every extra 100 hours. There must also be a recheck “each time the social media provider collects demographic information of any kind regarding the Indiana account holder.”

“These triggers are unrelated to any doubt about whether a user’s previous age verification was incorrect; they are simply burdens on extended engagement with speech on covered providers’ services,” says the complaint.

An account flagged as belonging to someone under 16 will get a notice within 7 days, and will be terminated in 30 days. The account can be saved if the user provides parental consent, or “any commercially reasonable method that relies on public or private transactional data to verify the age of the account holder.”

The law defines transactional data as “records that relate to a mortgage, education, or employment.”

In case neither of these avenues is taken, the platform “shall terminate the account at the conclusion of the thirty (30) day period.”

In case of parental consent, the information submitted for that purpose must be deleted “immediately after registering the individual’s provision of verifiable parental consent.” There is no such obligation for transactional records that are used to prove age.

As NetChoice noted, “the law requires no deletion of that data afterward.”

Regarding accounts of under-16s that are allowed to exist on social media because they have parental consent, the law prohibits platforms from showing them a feed based on their usage, including content, recommendations, or advertising. The account can only show up in searches by accounts “linked” to the adolescent’s.

Other restrictions include no “addictive” features such as infinite scroll, endless pages, like and share counts, autoplay, and live streaming. Another provision is that these accounts can only receive direct messages from “linked” accounts.

Parents will be given a separate password to monitor the account, set limits, and access it at any time.

NetChoice is not challenging at this time the direct message limit, nor the parental-password and supervision features – but reserves the right to do so if the state interprets the law as allowing parents to log in as the teen.

NetChoice is challenging the requirement to check age and residency at signup, the continuing age checks, the process of terminating accounts, and the restrictions on feeds and “addictive” features, as well as the search limit.

The filing also mentions other laws that have been blocked in various states, and the Supreme Court’s decision in the Free Speech Coalition v. Paxton case, which upheld Texas’s age checks for porn sites, but also said that requiring adults to prove their age “is a burden on the exercise of” First Amendment rights.

District courts in Utah, Arkansas, Virginia, and Nebraska have blocked similar laws, but their rulings are now on appeal. In June, the Sixth Circuit reversed a decision that had blocked Ohio’s parental-consent law, while the Eleventh Circuit allowed Florida’s HB 3 to stand.

NetChoice also relies on the high court’s Brown v. Entertainment Merchants (2011) and Packingham (2017) decisions, with the former stating that such laws “impose governmental authority, subject only to a parental veto.”

Taske noted that federal courts have blocked similar laws in several states, and expressed confidence that “Indiana’s law should fall too.”

HEA 1408 was approved almost unanimously, with a 93-0 vote in the House, and 49-1 in the Senate. Our tracker says that “Indiana wrote ongoing age monitoring of adults into law and called it child safety.”

In October, the Eleventh Circuit Court of Appeals allowed a similar law in Georgia to proceed, though the ruling was on procedure and did not address the law’s constitutionality.

In December 2025, Attorney General Rokita sued Aylo for not preventing users in Indiana from accessing its sites with the help of VPNs – even though the company had already blocked the state.

In June 2024, NetChoice sued Mississippi over its social media age checks law, while the porn industry challenged Indiana’s adult-site age verification law.

What all this means is that the legal battle over online age verification, and the way it affects both children and adults, is far from over.

It’s not just the frequency and the way these checks are performed that is the problem – but also the fact that the law treats spending time online as grounds for suspicion, and that the more you read and post, the more often you have to prove your age.

If an adult is wrongly flagged as a minor, they must hand over records that concern their mortgage, school, or job, in order to continue expressing themselves online – with no guarantee that this highly personal data will be deleted. That’s an identity system for speech, built in the name of children.

articles.title: USAID Files: Staff Said Taxpayers Were Footing Big Tech’s Disinformation Bill
articles.content:
If you're tired of censorship and surveillance, subscribe to Reclaim The Net.

In January 2021, two USAID officials, Lorri Anne Meils and Josh Machleder, discussed in a Google chat how their agency’s anti-"disinformation" efforts were effectively letting Big Tech – specifically, Facebook and Twitter – off the hook.

The fix, according to these bureaucrats, wasn’t to stop the government from financing projects that flag content for censorship, but to get the platforms to share the burden and start paying for it, too.

What USAID’s money is used for is to support local organizations that monitor and flag content to major social media platforms, as explained in a February 22, 2022, information memo prepared for the agency’s Administrator. The example given is Ethiopia, where USAID’s Office of Transition Initiatives (OTI) pays a local group for “biweekly social media monitoring reports” – which are then shared with the Global Engagement Center (GEC) at the State Department, and, as the memo has it, “who are in process of sharing them with Big Tech (Twitter, Facebook, YouTube) to flag false content or hate speech on their respective platforms.”

Another example is Ukraine and Moldova, where USAID’s work “enabled troll-hunting organizations to report more than 200 inauthentic accounts to Facebook, which later disabled these accounts.”

A one-pager for the "Friend or Foe?" program, piloted in Kenya in 2018-2019, states that its goal was to "counter disinformation efforts and support independent journalism through improving the signals that drive algorithmic decision-making in online platforms and that moderate or censor content." The program was carried out by Article 19, Meedan, NDI, and Graphika. The same document touches on the fairness of this work, noting that “the removal of legitimate and credible information” is a concern.

The conversation was part of the USAID Files released on the agency’s website in November 2026. The chat took place on Sunday, January 24, 2021, when Meils asked Machleder to help her come up with an “if asked” answer for a “murder board” they were preparing for a principal (who is never named in the chat).

Her premise was that “our work basically lets FB and Twitter off the hook for supporting these matters” and “forced the tax payers to bear the burden.”

Machleder’s response was to suggest that USAID work with the companies to make them pay more, rather than stop using taxpayer money to fund these projects. He wrote, “maybe suggesting a GDA or other way that US taxpayers aren’t completely footing the bill” – and added, “for the damage they cause.”

GDA stands for Global Development Alliance, a public-private partnership model that USAID uses to collaborate with private entities. Meils responded with “i LOVE a GDA”.

The chat does not mention the principal by name, and it’s not clear whether the cost sharing answer was ever used, or if a deal with Meta was ever signed at the terms mentioned in the documents. The two staff members were not whistleblowers in the sense that they wanted to stop the anti-disinformation work, but rather make sure that social media platforms pay more for it.

As Meils put it, “there needs to be some way higher leverage to squeeze cash out.”

The two officials were also under the impression that the platforms were giving only token financial support – $250,000 donations. She called this “bananas” and “totally extractive.”

Machleder’s contribution to the chat was to add that USAID “can and should consider burden-sharing arrangements with social media platforms to address these harms by financing activities to mitigate them.”

An undated draft confirmation Q&A prepared for a nominee - with a note in the margin saying it was "assigned to Joshua Machleder" - shows that the idea of making the platforms pay was developed into a potential answer to be given at a hearing.

The answer that was drafted is: “I believe it is important to cost-share with social media, and will explore such arrangements with social media platforms to address harms to democracy and human rights through jointly-financed activities to mitigate them.”

This included providing “cutting edge tools and skills to provide actionable data for social media platforms, such as Facebook” as well as “situation rooms” to monitor these platforms during elections.

The memo states, “USAID believes it should co-own foreign disinformation efforts because it overwhelmingly owns the relevant programming by dollar amount.”

The document reveals that USAID’s media-related programs in Ukraine alone had a budget of $60 million, including money spent on content monitoring.

Ahead of Power’s confirmation hearings, briefing notes said, “we need more resources given the scale of the crisis.”

A data sheet compiled in May 2021 with Machleder among the contributors, details some of the activities and their cost: $24.7 million for the Ukraine Transformation Communications Activity, implemented by Chemonics, described as promoting “alternative narratives.”

In Georgia, a $7.5 million program implemented by Zinc was set up to map disinformation sources and spread counter-messages. In Indonesia, USAID paid for custom software to find “socially harmful content.”

The data sheet doesn’t provide a reliable total of how much the anti-disinformation work costs, as it contains a mix of project ceilings, partial information, and blank spaces.

The data sheet does show that most of the activities are geared towards supporting journalism and media development, as well as media literacy. The memo from February 2022 states that the goal of the work is to build resilience “rather than engage in information/psychological operations.”

The goals for 2023, as stated in one of the documents, are to “reinforce tech partnerships with Google, Meta, and Microsoft to address information manipulation and other safety issues.”

There’s no mention of these companies paying a share of the cost – rather, USAID said it was looking for a new mechanism to fund activities with a ceiling of $20 million.

The documents also show that while the initial idea was to make the platforms pay more, at least in 2022, USAID was happy to partner with Meta (Facebook) on a digital literacy project in Indonesia, where the company would contribute less money than the agency.

In the first year of the activity, USAID was to contribute $250,000 in cash, while Meta would give $70,000 in cash and $180,000 “in-kind.” In the second year, USAID’s contribution would remain the same, while Meta’s cash contribution would rise to $100,000, and in-kind contribution to $150,000.

In the past, Reclaim The Net covered USAID's "Disinformation Primer" documents, the agency's extensive media empire, and the model used in Georgia to get accounts taken down, as well as trusted flaggers that nobody can audit.

It was not the fact that the US government was effectively using taxpayers’ money to fund the work of organizations that flagged content to Big Tech that bothered these two officials. The issue was that the platforms were not chipping in enough.

articles.title: Tor Browser flaw lets websites uncover users’ IP addresses
articles.content:
Security researchers demonstrated how a malicious website could make Tor Browser connect directly to an attacker’s server, exposing the visitor’s public IP address.

The attack worked on Tor Browser 15.0.22 with default settings and was blocked by a security update released in September.

Calif researcher Carlos Roque detailed the attack in a November 26 report, published as part of OpenAI’s Patch the Planet program. Roque demonstrated the attack on Linux. The website needed the visitor to click once because Tor Browser otherwise blocked the pop-up used in the test.

Tor Browser pairs a hardened version of Firefox with software that sends web traffic through the Tor network. When a user visits a regular website, the site sees the IP address of the Tor exit relay. A separate connection that bypasses Tor can expose the public IP address of the network the visitor is using, undermining the privacy Tor provides.

How the browser leaked the IP address

The demonstration started with CVE-2026-92027, a high-severity use-after-free flaw in Firefox’s Streams component. A use-after-free occurs when software continues to access memory after releasing it. In this case, the bug let the malicious page gain code execution inside the sandboxed process that handles web content.

From there, the attack abused the browser’s session history to get the main browser process to load a privileged developer tools page. That page opened a direct connection to the attacker’s server outside Tor. The server could log the source IP address as soon as the connection was established, while the site’s ordinary web requests continued to arrive through Tor.

The address the server saw depended on how the device reached the internet. A VPN or a network using address translation could cause the server to see the VPN’s or network’s public IP address. Calif’s report describes a proof of concept and does not indicate actual attacks against users.

Tor Browser users should update

Mozilla fixed the Streams vulnerability in Firefox ESR 140.16, which the Tor Project incorporated into Tor Browser 15.0.23 on September 15, 2026. The Tor Project released Tor Browser 16.0.3 on November 24 with additional Firefox security updates.

If you’re still running an older version, install the latest release available for your platform. On desktop, open the Tor Browser menu when the update prompt appears and choose “Update available – restart now.”

articles.title: Optimizing threat intelligence for security operations centers
articles.content:
Security operations centers often struggle with operational inefficiencies caused by poorly implemented threat intelligence sources, which can hinder rather than help detection efforts, as first reported by HackRead.

Many security teams face challenges when threat intelligence data lacks quality, arrives too late, or requires manual processing. Research indicates that relying on limited external visibility forces organizations to react only after threats reach their own environment. To address these gaps, security professionals are increasingly integrating automated threat intelligence feeds directly into existing security information and event management systems.

For instance, the ANY.RUN interactive sandbox platform provides indicators derived from real-world malware and phishing investigations across 16,000 organizations. By utilizing feeds that offer approximately 99% unique indicators of compromise and near-zero false positive rates, teams can expand their visibility beyond internal telemetry.

Furthermore, integrating these feeds into platforms like Microsoft Sentinel or Elastic Security allows for automated workflows, reducing the manual burden on analysts. Prioritizing timely, high-quality data integration enables security operations centers to improve detection coverage, preserve analyst capacity, and maximize the return on investment for their existing security infrastructure.

Source: HackRead

articles.title: Drupal sites are being hijacked, and a follow-up flaw is already under attack
articles.content:
.kadence-column493050_1502b1-e5 > .kadence-column493050_1502b1-e5 > .kadence-column493050_1502b1-e5 > .kadence-column493050_1502b1-e5 > .kt-inside-inner-col > .kadence-column493050_1502b1-e5 > .kadence-column493050_1502b1-e5 > .kt-inside-inner-col:before{opacity:0.3;}@media all and (max-width: 1024px){.kadence-column493050_1502b1-e5 > }@media all and (max-width: 767px){.kadence-column493050_1502b1-e5 > }

In this article

  • A hijacked website can expose your personal data or serve phishing pages and malicious downloads
  • Attackers are exploiting two critical Drupal flaws to take over websites
  • Drupal site owners should install the latest security update and check for signs of a break-in

Attackers are exploiting a second critical flaw in Drupal, the content management system (CMS) behind many government, university, corporate, and media websites. Site owners are responsible for applying the fix. For visitors, a hijacked site can put personal data and devices at risk.

On November 18, Drupal released a patch for a remote code execution (RCE) flaw, CVE-2026-132165. The flaw could let attackers take over a site by abusing Drupal’s installer file, install.php. Drupal’s security team received a report of attacks on live sites as early as November 19.

On November 25, Drupal released a second advisory for CVE-2026-136716. Some sites in “unusual or incomplete install states” remained vulnerable to takeover after the first fix, including live sites. Drupal says the new flaw is also being exploited in the wild.

These flaws is a serious problem for website owners, because:

  • No login is needed. Anonymous attackers can exploit the first flaw. They can attempt to reinstall Drupal and gain control of the site or run code on the server.
  • Hard to spot. Drupal says the user interface doesn’t show whether a site is in the vulnerable state. Already-compromised sites may no longer show as vulnerable.
  • Already exploited. CISA added the first flaw to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog and gave federal agencies until November 27 to fix it.
  • Drupal has a history of abuse. CISA has flagged six Drupal flaws as exploited since November 2021. Two of them were used in ransomware attacks.

How to stay safe

A hijacked site could expose data stored there, such as account details, email addresses, and form submissions. Attackers could also serve phishing pages or malicious downloads from a trusted domain or deface the site.

Scam or legit? Scam Guard knows.

TRY IT NOW

If you’re a visitor or customer:

  • Be wary of unexpected login prompts, “verify your account” pop-ups, or surprise downloads on sites you normally trust.
  • Use unique passwords and a password manager. If a site you use reports a breach, change that password and anywhere you reused it.
  • Turn on multi-factor authentication where it’s offered.
  • Keep your operating system, browser, and security software up to date.
  • Treat emails that cite a “security incident” with caution. Go to the site directly instead of clicking links.

If you run a Drupal site:

  • Update to Drupal 10.6.23, 11.3.23, or 11.4.14, then run update.php. Drupal says an update hook must run to fix existing production sites.
  • Block access to /core/install.php in your web server configuration or .htaccess file if you can’t upgrade right away.
  • Check your logs for unexpected changes to or by the user 1 account (the first account created when a site is installed). Make sure you control the email address on that account, and consider resetting its password.
  • If you suspect a break-in, follow Drupal’s guide to responding to a hacked site.
  • Drupal 10.5 and earlier 10.x releases, and Drupal 11.2 and earlier 11.x releases, have reached end of life. Move to a supported release to receive security fixes.
  • Sites protected by the paid Drupal Steward service are covered against known attack vectors, but Drupal still recommends upgrading.

Patching alone may not be enough. A compromised site can still look normal after patching, so site owners should update Drupal and check for signs of a break-in.

articles.title: CVE-2026-104286: Fortinet FortiMail path traversal enables file writes in HTTP request handling (Update: Nuclei template published)
articles.content:
Fortinet FortiMail path traversal enables file writes in HTTP request handling

Affects Fortinet FortiMail 7.0.0 through 7.0.9, 7.2.0-7.2.9, 7.4.0-7.4.8, 7.6.0-7.6.6 and 8.0.0-8.0.1. Fixed in 8.0.2, 7.6.7, 7.4.9 and 7.2.10; no fix version is listed for 7.0.

9.8CriticalCNA

  • Exploited
  • Yes, on CISA KEV
  • Fix
  • Fixed in 8.0.2, 7.6.7, 7.4.9, 7.2.10
  • Who is exposed
  • Not reported

Summary

A path traversal flaw in Fortinet FortiMail lets an attacker write arbitrary files on the underlying system, which Fortinet rates as able to lead to unauthorized code or command execution. It can be reached remotely, without logging in, by sending crafted HTTP or HTTPS requests, and it is being exploited in attacks.

Written by a model

Original description

An improper limitation of a pathname to a restricted directory ('path traversal') vulnerability in Fortinet FortiMail 8.0.0 through 8.0.1, FortiMail 7.6.0 through 7.6.6, FortiMail 7.4.0 through 7.4.8, FortiMail 7.2.0 through 7.2.9, FortiMail 7.0 all versions may allow an unauthenticated attacker to write arbitrary files on the underlying system via crafted HTTP or HTTPS requests.

What to do

  1. Upgrade to a fixed version: 8.0.2, 7.6.7, 7.4.9, 7.2.10.

  2. Workaround: Disable the IBE feature (Encryption -> IBE -> IBE Service off, or 'config system encryption ibe / set status disable'). Alternatively, block internet access to the webmail interface or limit it to trusted private networks, or block POST requests to /ibe containing '../' on a WAF.

  3. Fix it by , CISA's deadline for US federal agencies.

    CISA's required action: Apply mitigations in accordance with vendor instructions, ensuring compliance with CISA’s BOD 26-04 Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk (see URL in Notes) guidance and CISA’s “Forensics Triage Requirements” (see URL in Notes). Follow applicable BOD 26-04 guidance for cloud services or discontinue use of the product if mitigations are unavailable. Stakeholders are responsible for evaluating each asset's internet exposure and ensuring adherence to BOD 26-04 patching guidelines.

Check your systems with an agent

Paste this into a coding or ops agent. It checks your systems read-only and reports a table per asset.

Check whether my systems are affected by CVE-2026-104286 (An improper limitation of a pathname to a restricted directory ('path traversal') vulnerability in Fortinet FortiMail 8.0.0 through 8.0.1…), using the cve.now data below.

Rules: work read-only. Do not run exploit code, proof-of-concept scripts or scanners that send attack payloads, and do not change any configuration, package, image or deployment. Report findings only.

What cve.now has for CVE-2026-104286 (entry last updated 2026-10-28):
Affected:
- Fortinet FortiMail: from 8.0.0, through 8.0.1; from 7.6.0, through 7.6.6; from 7.4.0, through 7.4.8; from 7.2.0, through 7.2.9; from 7.0.0, through 7.0.9
Fixed versions: 8.0.2, 7.6.7, 7.4.9, 7.2.10.
Conditions (all must be true for the bug to be hit):
- Attacker can send crafted HTTP or HTTPS requests to the appliance (source: https://fortiguard.fortinet.com/psirt/FG-IR-26-175)
Setup: unknown whether the bug needs a non-default feature or setting. Check the advisory.
Attacker needs: network access, no login, no user action.
Workaround: Disable the IBE feature (Encryption -> IBE -> IBE Service off, or 'config system encryption ibe / set status disable'). Alternatively, block internet access to the webmail interface or limit it to trusted private networks, or block POST requests to /ibe containing '../' on a WAF. (source: https://www.cve.org/CVERecord?id=CVE-2026-104286)
CISA KEV: CVE-2026-104286 is listed as known exploited (added 2026-10-01, remediation due 2026-10-04). CISA's required action: Apply mitigations in accordance with vendor instructions, ensuring compliance with CISA’s BOD 26-04 Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk (see URL in Notes) guidance and CISA’s “Forensics Triage Requirements” (see URL in Notes). Follow applicable BOD 26-04 guidance for cloud services or discontinue use of the product if mitigations are unavailable. Stakeholders are responsible for evaluating each asset's internet exposure and ensuring adherence to BOD 26-04 patching guidelines.
This KEV status is for CVE-2026-104286 only. If you also check another CVE, look up its own KEV status; never assume it from this one.

How to check:
- Installed software: check what is actually running, not what a repo declares. Read the version from each host, container image and Kubernetes node (the binary's version output, the OS package database, image layers), and check whether the conditions above hold there. Distribution packages may carry a backported fix under an older version number; confirm against the distribution's own advisory.

Verify against the linked advisories before concluding, and cite the date you read each one:
- https://fortiguard.fortinet.com/psirt/FG-IR-26-175
- https://www.cisa.gov/known-exploited-vulnerabilities-catalog?field_cve=CVE-2026-104286

Do not conclude an asset is unaffected unless you checked it and the evidence covers both its version and the conditions above. If you could not check something, mark it unknown and say what is missing.

articles.title: 1Password reports security incident involving corporate GitHub account
articles.content:
1Password recently experienced a backend security breach after an unauthorized party gained access to a staff member's corporate GitHub account, as reported by Infosecurity Magazine.

The company initiated an investigation on Nov. 19 after detecting suspicious activity. The attacker utilized the compromised GitHub credentials to inject malicious code into backend services, allowing them to access administrative records for a subset of users. While the breach involved private repository code and the company's continuous integration and continuous delivery system, 1Password confirmed that customer vault contents remained secure.

Exposed data included user names, email addresses, account IDs and Secure Remote Password protocol parameters. A small number of users also had invitation and recovery tokens exposed. In response, 1Password revoked the compromised credentials, rotated infrastructure secrets and implemented stricter security controls. The firm also increased the length of invitation and recovery codes from six to 10 characters as a precautionary measure.

Although no evidence suggests that the stolen tokens were used to hijack accounts, the company advised users to remain vigilant against potential phishing attempts. 1Password stated that customers do not need to take further action, as the company continues to work with external security experts to verify its containment efforts.

Source: Infosecurity Magazine

articles.title: Malware steals Gmail messages using a fake Google Sheets extension
articles.content:
.kadence-column493015_22c4a9-7b > .kadence-column493015_22c4a9-7b > .kadence-column493015_22c4a9-7b > .kadence-column493015_22c4a9-7b > .kt-inside-inner-col > .kadence-column493015_22c4a9-7b > .kadence-column493015_22c4a9-7b > .kt-inside-inner-col:before{opacity:0.3;}@media all and (max-width: 1024px){.kadence-column493015_22c4a9-7b > }@media all and (max-width: 767px){.kadence-column493015_22c4a9-7b > }

In this article

  • Remus malware installs a Chrome extension disguised as Google Sheets
  • The extension can resume stealing unread Gmail messages when you sign back in on the infected device
  • If you suspect an infection, check your Chrome extensions and secure your Google Account from a clean device

In our earlier post about Remus, we covered the claim that the infostealer could read your Gmail even after you changed your password. New research from Gen Threat Labs traced the supposed Gmail “zero-day” to a Chrome extension that masquerades as Google Sheets. The malicious extension stays installed after a password change and can start reading your mail again when you sign back in on the infected device.

On November 8, the developers of the Remus infostealer began advertising a Gmail “zero-day.” They said it gave access to a victim’s mailbox even after they changed their password and signed out of all sessions.

Gen Threat Labs published its findings on November 24. The researchers found no email-stealing code in the main stealer. That lives in a separate module that Remus downloads from the attackers’ server when the malware runs. The developers advertised the feature as exclusive to their $1,000-a-month Enterprise tier.

The module is a native DLL whose only job is to install a malicious extension in Google Chrome, the only browser it targets. It edits the victim’s Chrome profile files to register the extension and recalculates the integrity checks that protect those files. It also turns on Developer mode, which Chrome requires to run unpacked extensions.

The extension calls itself “Google Sheets” and copies the description of the Google Docs Offline extension. It requests access to all websites. Every minute, it checks Gmail for unread messages, retrieves the contents, and then sends the subject, body, sender, and your email address to the attackers.

So, the password change claim is true?

Only partly. When you sign out or end your Gmail session, the extension stops reading your mail. But it stays installed in Chrome. As soon as you sign back in on the infected device with your new password, it can start reading your mail again.

You might never notice it. The visible clues are a new extension card and the Developer mode switch turned on. But it’s still a persistence trick and a marketing pitch, not a Google vulnerability. Malware able to install an extension silently could just as easily steal your session cookies directly. Which doesn’t make it any less dangerous. Especially when your inbox holds password-reset links and verification codes for your other accounts.

What to do

If you think your device may be infected with an infostealer:

  • Clean the device. The extension can start reading your mail again if you sign back in on the infected computer. Scan with an up-to-date anti-malware solution, and use a separate, clean device to change your Google password.
  • Check your extensions. Enter chrome://extensions in your address bar. Look for extensions you don’t recognize or no longer use. The fake “Google Sheets” extension is marked as unpacked, meaning it was loaded from local files. Google’s real Docs Offline extension is only available from the Chrome Web Store. Remove anything suspicious.
  • Check Developer Mode. On the same page, look for the Developer mode toggle in the top-right corner. If it’s on (and buttons like Load unpacked appear) and you didn’t turn it on, treat that as a red flag.
  • Secure your Google account. When you’re sure your device is clean, change your password, sign out of all devices, and review your recovery options, connected apps, and Gmail forwarding rules and filters.
  • Review accounts tied to that inbox. Look for unexpected changes, starting with accounts that use your Gmail address for sign-in or recovery. Where available, enable multi-factor authentication or set up a passkey.

To stay safe in the future, only download software from trusted sources. Cracked software and fake installers are common ways infostealers reach your device.

Malwarebytes detects components of Remus as Trojan.Downloader.Ext and Spyware.Remus.

Cybersecurity risks should never spread beyond a headline. Keep threats off your devices by downloading Malwarebytes today.

articles.title: In Other News: Tanker Cyberattacks, EU Quantum Act, New VirusTotal Capabilities
articles.content:
SecurityWeek’s weekly cybersecurity news roundup offers a concise overview of important developments that may not receive full standalone coverage yet remain relevant to the broader threat landscape.

This curated summary highlights key stories across vulnerability disclosures, emerging attack methods, policy updates, industry reports, and other noteworthy events to help readers stay well-informed about the evolving cybersecurity environment.

Here are this week’s highlights: 

ChatGPT Sites exposure

Pluto researchers combed web archives, public code repositories, search engines and other sources and found 16,666 sites created with ChatGPT Sites (which builds and hosts web apps for ChatGPT and Codex users), 12,830 of which were accessible to anyone. Manual checks confirmed sensitive data exposure at 27 organizations, including a Fortune 500 company’s sales dashboard, a freight forwarder’s customer quotes, and a vendor’s sales pitch. Sites are visible only to their owners and admins unless shared, but owners can open them to the entire internet.

RansomwareHelp co-founder accused of profiting from ransom payments

US authorities have charged Juan Ricardo Palacio Escobar, a Colombian national and co-founder of the ransomware recovery firm RansomwareHelp, with three counts of wire fraud. Prosecutors allege that instead of using its own decryption technology as advertised, his company purchased decryptors from cybercriminals at prices significantly lower than what it charged customers. In one case involving undercover FBI agents, Palacio allegedly paid a $6,000 ransom and billed the purported victim $13,260 for decrypting their files.

USDA payment systems breach

A system used by the US Department of Agriculture (USDA) to make payments to farmers has been breached, according to NBC News. Two former department officials said the intrusion could let hackers access databases containing sensitive information on food safety and diseases carried by animals.

SolarWinds and Adobe patch vulnerabilities

SolarWinds has patched several critical vulnerabilities in its Serv-U managed file transfer product, including flaws that can lead to privilege escalation and arbitrary code execution. Adobe has addressed critical security holes in Campaign Classic and Experience Manager, including ones that allow arbitrary code execution, and a medium-severity DoS vulnerability in InDesign.

Container Store restores systems after cyberattack

US retailer The Container Store has restored its systems following a cyberattack that prevented customers from placing orders online. There is currently no evidence that customers’ financial information was stolen. The n0n ransomware group listed the company on its leak site earlier this month, but The Container Store has not addressed the claim.

VirusTotal adds new ransomware detection capabilities

VirusTotal has introduced new ransomware detection capabilities that rely on evidence of user files being encrypted during sandbox analysis. The improvements include a new behavior tag and stricter requirements for assigning the MITRE ATT&CK technique associated with data encryption for impact. VirusTotal demonstrated the effectiveness of the changes against ransomware that evaded detection by all 75 static antivirus engines at the time of analysis.

$17 billion targeted in US government anti-scam operation

The US Justice Department’s crackdown on fraud has targeted more than 800 defendants across over 400 cases since March. Authorities have also helped disrupt scam centers in more than 10 countries. According to the FBI, its Operation Blackout has led to the seizure or restraint of nearly $17 billion.

McDonald’s Japan hacked

McDonald’s Japan has disclosed a breach involving a database storing information associated with its mobile application. Hackers gained access to customer purchase histories, device location information, internal customer identifiers and IP addresses, but not names, contact details or credit card data. The number of impacted customers has not been disclosed.

Bithumb uncovers wider breach

South Korean cryptocurrency exchange Bithumb says more individuals and more types of personal information were compromised in an October cyberattack than initially reported. Bithumb also said the hackers had access for more than two weeks, not one hour as initially believed. The hackers stole data from an internal collaboration system, including identity documents, bank account numbers, transaction histories, and crypto wallet addresses. South Korean media reported that the initial victim count exceeded 7,000, including customers and staff.

Artex gains traction among state-sponsored hackers

Microsoft has observed several state-sponsored hacking groups, including China’s Salt Typhoon, as well as cybercriminals using the AI-powered penetration testing framework Artex. Hackers have leveraged the tool to identify exposed secrets in public code repositories, conduct supply chain attacks and find vulnerable systems. Microsoft says the framework can significantly accelerate intrusions, with attackers achieving privileged access and establishing persistence within minutes.

Quantum Act targets Europe’s cryptographic readiness

The European Commission’s proposed Quantum Act includes measures to accelerate the development and adoption of post-quantum cryptography and prepare the EU for the security risks posed by quantum computers. The legislation is part of a broader effort to strengthen Europe’s quantum technology industry, reduce reliance on foreign suppliers and establish global leadership in the field by 2030.

Tanker cyberattacks 

Up to 50 ships carrying oil, liquefied petroleum, chemicals and other potentially dangerous cargo are believed to have been targeted in a wave of cyberattacks, according to The Wall Street Journal. US authorities are investigating whether Iran is responsible for the attacks.

Radware hacked

An internal report obtained by BleepingComputer shows that hackers breached cybersecurity firm Radware through an unprotected Cloud WAF management API exposed to the internet. Customer contact information and credentials associated with AWS, Azure and SFTP storage used by some customers may have been compromised. The company has not responded to SecurityWeek’s request for comment.

Related: In Other News: New CISA Director Nominee, Connected Car Hacking, Baker Tilly Data Breach
