articles.title: 100,000 Potentially Impacted by Colorado Data Breach
articles.content:
The Colorado Governor’s Office of Information Technology (OIT) has disclosed a data breach impacting data that residents uploaded to the myColorado application.

Colorado’s official mobile application, myColorado is used for digital identification, state services, and document storage. It has approximately 2.1 million users.

OIT took the application offline last week, after identifying unauthorized access to platform data, and immediately initiated incident response and an investigation into the incident.

One week after the outage began, OIT said it discovered the incident after the attackers triggered the automated threat detection systems deployed within its Amazon Web Services (AWS) environment.

The investigation has determined that the attackers accessed documents stored within the ‘myCards and Documents’ section of the application, which includes user-uploaded data, such as PDF files and photos of government IDs, vehicle registrations, and insurance cards.

According to Colorado, approximately 100,000 individuals might have been affected, but no payment information was accessed.

“Staff are working around the clock to match the inappropriately accessed documents to individual users. As that matching continues, OIT will further refine estimates on the number of people whose data was involved,” Colorado said.

The myColorado application remains offline and OIT has not announced a restoration date. The state expects to start sending direct notifications to the affected individuals on November 27.

“Our main goal is to protect the security of users. Additionally, we are prioritizing direct notification of users involved in the incident and getting the app up and running as soon as possible, with security enhancements in place,” said state CIO and OIT executive director Sarah Tuneberg.

articles.title: Hex Package Manager Warns of Potential Data Breach
articles.content:
Hex, the package manager for Elixir and Erlang, fell victim to a cyberattack involving unauthorized access to its web servers.

The incident occurred on November 23, when the attackers exploited a vulnerability in hex.pm to execute commands. The attack was immediately blocked, and the underlying security defect was addressed within 20 minutes.

Between 18:16 and 18:29 UTC, the attacker sent 69 malicious requests, affecting six web servers. At 18:30, Hex replaced all hex.pm servers with patched versions rejecting the payload, and its firewall rule fully blocked the attacker’s traffic at 18:33.

“We found no evidence of unauthorized package modifications, database changes, or that the attacker maintained access to our systems,” the package manager explains.

According to Hex, potential access to database contents, such as email addresses, password hashes, API key hashes, sessions, second factor authentication secrets, and audit logs, cannot be ruled out.

While all the observed reads of private packages came from Hex servers, any read from a compromised server would appear legitimate, it says. Additionally, database and private documentation reads are not logged, hindering visibility into potential data exposure.

“The attacker’s commands could read the credentials our servers use, so we replaced them: the storage, CDN, email and database credentials, and the keys that sign sessions and access tokens. This logged everyone out of hex.pm and Hex clients,” Hex notes.

The package manager has been working on a new registry signing system with key rotation support. Until new Hex client iterations are rolled out, users should avoid fetching packages from third-party mirrors and rely only on repo.hex.pm.

Hex also recommends that all account holders change their hex.pm passwords and reset their two-factor authentication.

“Because email addresses may have been exposed, be careful with emails that claim to come from Hex. Please double-check that the links they contain lead to hex.pm,” the package manager says.

The attackers exploited an unauthenticated deserialization of untrusted data bug (tracked as CVE-2026-129514, CVSS score of 10) that allowed them to execute OS commands via a crafted Erlang external term format request body and gain remote code execution (RCE).

Hex discovered that the Ash Framework was also impacted by the same class of vulnerability. Ash patched the flaw (tracked as CVE-2026-124283) on November 24, warning it could lead to code execution or SQL injection.

Associated security defects were also patched in two other Elixir libraries: namely db_connection (CVE-2026-133555) and flop (CVE-2026-130411).

articles.title: SAP Confirms Cyberattack, Source Code Reportedly Compromised
articles.content:
Enterprise software giant SAP has confirmed it is investigating a cybersecurity incident following reports that threat actors targeted its development infrastructure.

German publication Der Spiegel [paywalled] broke the news on Thursday, citing SAP insiders and an internal notification sent to employees.

SAP told SecurityWeek that it had detected suspicious activity and implemented measures to protect customers and secure its services. The German company did not disclose details of the attack.

“Based on our investigation to date, we have found no evidence of unauthorized access to customer business data,” SAP told SecurityWeek.

German news agency DPA reviewed internal SAP communications that revealed the suspicious activity had been identified within GitHub.

According to an insider cited by Der Spiegel, the hackers obtained SAP employees’ authentication tokens, enabling them to copy and alter source code stored on GitHub.

SAP publishes developer tools, sample applications, and open source projects on GitHub. It’s unclear whether the threat actor accessed any proprietary code.

Separately, Handelsblatt reported that SAP’s emergency security measures have affected numerous teams. The software giant has reportedly replaced signing keys, limited access to GitHub, and suspended automated development operations.

None of the reports indicate that tampered code was incorporated into software delivered to SAP customers.

Sources cited by Der Spiegel suggested that the attack may have been assisted by AI. While AI involvement has not been confirmed, several major organizations, including the European Commission, have recently disclosed AI-assisted cyberattacks.

In late October, the Gentlemen ransomware group listed SAP on its leak website, pointing to the company’s Latin American operations. File listings reviewed by SecurityWeek suggest the hackers obtained SAP-related software and source code, but it is unclear whether SAP itself or a third party was compromised. The two incidents do not appear to be connected.

articles.title: Christian Evangelist Thrown From Boat And Drowned In Uganda
articles.content:
by Stefan J. Bos, Worthy News Chief International Correspondent

KAMPALA (Worthy News) – A Christian father of three has died in Uganda, where Muslims threw him off a water taxi after he shared the Gospel with passengers, well-informed Christians said Thursday.

Gilbert Musede, 32, of Kaliro Town Council, reportedly drowned on November 5 after five men, a witness identified as Muslims, threw him from a passenger boat into Lake Lemwa in eastern Uganda’s Kibuku District.

Anna Maria Nausimba, one of the passengers, told Christian news agency Morning Star News that Musede was a member of Discipleship Church of Christ in Kaliro.

Nausimba said she met Musede earlier that day when they boarded a taxi in Namwiwa. They later took the same boat across Lake Lemwa. When a storm broke out during the crossing, Musede stood and prayed for it to pass, she said. The weather improved, and the boat continued.

WITNESS DESCRIBES ATTACK

Nausimba recalled that Musede spoke to passengers about his Christian faith, referring to the Bible and the Quran, which Muslims consider holy. Five men took offense, she stressed. One, whom she heard others call Shakuuru, allegedly stood and shouted, “Allahu Akbar,” Arabic for “Allah is greatest.”

She said he then invoked the biblical account of Jonah, a prophet who was thrown into the sea during a storm, swallowed by a great fish and returned alive to dry land after three days.

The men challenged Musede to prove his faith by surviving in the water, accused him of preaching false teachings and threw him overboard, Nausimba said.

Nausimba said the men ordered the boat operator to turn back and left on motorcycles after reaching shore. She appealed for help, and local divers and fishermen recovered Musede’s body about six hours later, she said.

CHRISTIAN CONVERTS PRESSURED

Musede was on his way to visit friends when he died, Christians said. He is survived by his wife and three children.

Musede’s family and church were reportedly gathering information to take to police. Whether police opened an investigation remained unclear Thursday.

Christian advocacy group Open Doors has identified eastern Uganda, where the tragedy occurred, as an area where converts from Islam to Christianity face particular pressure, including “harassment and rejection by relatives.”

Though the constitution of Uganda protects freedom of religion, anti-Christian attacks have continued, Worthy News documented.

The East African country’s 2024 census recorded about 38 million Christians and 6.05 million Muslims, roughly 82 percent and 13 percent of its 45.9 million people, respectively.

articles.title: The End of Man: The Real Danger Isn’t Artificial Intelligence
articles.content:
The End of Man: The Real Danger Isn’t Artificial Intelligence

“Things fall apart; the centre cannot hold.”
W.B. Yeats, “The Second Coming”

We have been suffering through a veritable cascade of technological failures.

First came a massive Microsoft outage that disrupted Outlook and other online services around the globe.

Then came a nationwide ground stop that brought air travel across America to a standstill, disrupting thousands of flights and leaving travelers stranded.

Then major banks experienced problems with their online systems.

Then United Airlines grounded departing flights after yet another computer failure.

Then reports that the highly classified network that the National Security Agency uses for its internal communications had gone down.

Then Apple joined the growing list of technology giants experiencing widespread disruptions, with users reporting problems accessing iCloud, the App Store, Apple Music and other services.

One breakdown after another. Communications disrupted. Transportation paralyzed. Financial services interrupted. Sensitive information potentially at risk. Millions of Americans reminded just how dependent their daily lives have become on technologies they neither understand nor control.

This is what happens when technology goes haywire.

Or is it?

Speculation was quick to point the finger at artificial intelligence, especially in the wake of the nationwide airline shutdown.

After all, the Trump administration had only recently expanded the FAA’s new SMART artificial-intelligence system to air traffic control centers across the country.

The administration has also been aggressively promoting AI (or SI for Super Intelligence as Trump insists it be called) as the answer to everything from government inefficiency to national security, even as it pushes to reduce regulatory barriers and expand the use of automated systems.

Yet the Trump administration insists AI had nothing to do with the airline shutdown.

Instead, federal officials blamed the disruption on a malfunction involving aging air traffic control infrastructure, with problems arising as equipment was being replaced and communications systems updated.

Perhaps so.

Meanwhile, the FBI issued a report about another technological danger: autonomous AI hacking tools such as Artex AI that are being used to launch cyberattacks across the U.S. and globally and breach networks in under three hours.

But whether the culprit is artificial intelligence, cyberattackers, outdated equipment, poor planning, inadequate maintenance, human error or some combination of these factors, the larger problem remains.

Who is responsible when the technological systems upon which society depends begin to fail?

Who is accountable when government officials and corporate executives rush to embrace new technologies without ensuring that the safeguards, infrastructure and human oversight needed to manage them are in place?

And what happens when we become so dependent on technology—and so willing to surrender responsibility for managing it—that we can no longer distinguish between the failure of a machine and the failure of the human beings entrusted with its operation?

We’ve been asking the wrong question about artificial intelligence.

Maybe the real danger isn’t that machines might become smarter than human beings.

Maybe it’s the human hunger for power—and our willingness to surrender control to those who wield it.

Hollywood has spent decades warning us about machines that might someday become so intelligent, so independent and so powerful that they no longer need human beings.

In Stanley Kubrick’s 2001: A Space Odyssey, the seemingly infallible computer HAL 9000 turns against the astronauts who have entrusted their lives to its control. The machine, designed to serve humanity, becomes a threat to the very people it was created to assist.

Yet the more unsettling vision may come from an unlikely source: Pixar’s animated children’s film WALL-E. In WALL-E, humanity has abandoned an uninhabitable Earth and retreated to a massive spaceship where nearly every human need is anticipated and satisfied by machines.

People no longer walk. They no longer work. They barely notice the world around them. They are entertained, fed, transported and distracted by systems that make virtually every decision for them. They have become passive consumers of their own existence.

The machines haven’t needed to wage war against humanity. Human beings have largely surrendered their independence willingly, trading responsibility for convenience and freedom for comfort. Even the ship’s captain must struggle to reclaim his authority from an automated system programmed to maintain the status quo.

The distinction is telling.

In 2001, the nightmare is a machine that refuses to surrender control. In WALL-E, the nightmare is a humanity that has forgotten how to exercise it. Both films arrive at a troubling truth: technology becomes dangerous when human beings cease to exercise meaningful control over it.

And therein lies the problem: we have confused technological progress with human progress.

We have become extraordinarily adept at inventing machines capable of performing tasks that earlier generations could scarcely imagine.

We can split atoms, launch rockets into space, communicate instantaneously across continents, map the human genome, monitor populations from satellites and build computers capable of processing staggering amounts of information. Yet none of these technological achievements has necessarily made us wiser, more compassionate, more ethical or more capable of exercising restraint.

History demonstrates how readily human beings turn their greatest inventions into instruments of destruction, exploitation and control.

Consider the atomic bomb.

The discovery of nuclear fission opened the door to extraordinary scientific advances. It also made possible weapons capable of obliterating entire cities.

In August 1945, the United States dropped atomic bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki, killing tens of thousands of people immediately and many more in the aftermath.

The bombs did not decide to destroy those cities. Human beings did.

The same technology that made it possible to launch rockets into space also made possible missiles capable of delivering nuclear warheads across continents.

The same computers that revolutionized medicine, science, education and communication have helped give rise to a surveillance state capable of monitoring and tracking entire populations.

The internet, once hailed as an instrument of free expression and democratized knowledge, has also become a tool for collecting personal information, manipulating behavior and monitoring dissent.

Cameras become instruments of surveillance. Databases become tools for profiling and targeting people. Drones become weapons of remote warfare.

And now artificial intelligence threatens to magnify all of these capabilities, allowing governments, corporations and criminals to monitor, manipulate and control human behavior on an unprecedented scale.

The technology may be new, but the human impulses driving its misuse are as old as civilization itself.

Consider the FBI’s latest warning about ARTEX, an artificial-intelligence tool originally developed to help cybersecurity professionals identify weaknesses in computer networks.

In the hands of cybercriminals, that same technology has become a weapon.

According to the FBI, hackers have used ARTEX to automate cyberattacks against financial institutions, government agencies and private companies, with some attacks progressing from initial targeting to privileged access in less than three hours.

Meanwhile, Google’s Threat Intelligence Group warns that malicious actors are increasingly deploying autonomous AI systems capable of identifying vulnerabilities and carrying out attacks at machine speed, with dramatically reduced human intervention.

Think about that.

Technology intended to identify security weaknesses and protect computer networks is being turned into a weapon for exploiting those weaknesses.

The machines didn’t suddenly develop criminal intentions. Human beings created the tools, identified the targets and put the systems to work.

Artificial intelligence has not eliminated human greed, arrogance or the lust for power. It has given those impulses greater reach, greater speed and greater power.

We cannot afford to ignore the human beings behind the machines: the people who create the systems, finance them, deploy them, profit from them and look the other way when those systems are used to violate human rights.

And we especially cannot afford to ignore those who wield these technologies in the name of government.

Increasingly, we find ourselves navigating a world in which government agencies defer to computers as intermediaries in the relationship between the government and the populace.

We are being told to accept computerized decisions because they appear objective. We are urged to surrender personal information because convenience seems more important than privacy. We are persuaded to permit automated systems to make consequential judgments about human lives because questioning those systems requires effort, expertise and vigilance.

And we are forced to deal with the consequences of a government that treats anything generated by a computer as evidence that must be correct.

But computers can be wrong. Algorithms can be biased. Databases can contain errors. Automated systems can perpetuate and magnify the mistakes, prejudices and political agendas of those who build and operate them.

Greed turns technological advances into opportunities for exploitation.

Personal data becomes a commodity. Human behavior becomes something to be predicted, manipulated and monetized. The promise of greater efficiency becomes justification for cutting costs, eliminating human safeguards and concentrating even more power in fewer hands.

And when something goes wrong, the consequences are borne not necessarily by those who profited from the technology, but by the ordinary people whose lives depend upon it.

Arrogance and the quest for power convince those in power that technological capability is a green light to proceed.

Because the government can monitor communications, it assumes it should. Because it can track people’s movements, it does. Because it can deploy drones, predictive algorithms, facial recognition systems and increasingly autonomous weapons, it does.

But the ability to do something has never been the same as the right to do it.

The government does not acquire a constitutional exemption merely because its abuses are carried out by a computer rather than a human being. Indeed, the more powerful the technology, the greater the need for meaningful restraints on the people who control it.

Fifty years ago, the Senate’s Church Committee exposed extensive abuses by America’s intelligence agencies, including surveillance operations directed against citizens exercising their constitutional rights.

The warning was unmistakable: government power, particularly when exercised secretly and without effective oversight, can become a direct threat to the freedoms it is supposed to protect.

That was 1976.

Today, the surveillance capabilities available to government agencies would have been almost unimaginable to the officials investigated half a century ago.

Yet the constitutional questions remain the same.

Who watches the watchers? What happens to the Fourth Amendment and due process when surveillance and decisions affecting liberty are entrusted to opaque technological systems? Who holds the government accountable when it uses technology to circumvent the constitutional restraints meant to keep its power in check?

These are not merely technological questions. They are questions about power, freedom and human responsibility.

Forty years ago, in 1986, I explored many of these concerns in my book The End of Man.

At a time when artificial intelligence seemed largely confined to laboratories and science fiction, I devoted a chapter to the implications of creating machines that might increasingly shape—and potentially diminish—our understanding of what it means to be human.

The concern was not simply that computers might someday become powerful enough to dominate society. It was that human beings themselves were increasingly being reduced to systems of information, objects to be classified, studied, managed and manipulated.

As I warned then, “Man is not a machine.”

Human beings are more than information processors, data points or collections of predictable behaviors. Our humanity is bound up with our capacity for compassion, conscience, independent judgment and moral responsibility.

Yet even forty years ago, we were beginning to view ourselves as little more than machines.

The question I posed then remains just as urgent today: “How will we view ourselves tomorrow?”

Four decades later, that tomorrow has arrived.

We have become increasingly willing to allow machines to make decisions we should be questioning, corporations to manipulate information and governments to acquire surveillance powers that would have horrified earlier generations.

And when those systems fail—or are deliberately used to violate our rights—we allow the people responsible to hide behind the technology itself. “The computer made the mistake,” “the algorithm flagged the wrong person,” “the database contained an error,” “the artificial intelligence made the decision”—as if the machine were an independent moral actor, rather than a system designed, deployed and controlled by human beings.

There is an important difference between a machine that fails and a human being who refuses to accept responsibility for its failure.

This is precisely why the Constitution matters.

The Bill of Rights was not written for a world of artificial intelligence, facial recognition, mass data collection or automated warfare. It was written for a world in which human beings, entrusted with power, could not always be trusted to exercise that power responsibly.

Greed remains greed. Arrogance remains arrogance. And tyranny does not become less dangerous simply because it is administered by an algorithm.

Nor can we expect technology to rescue us from the moral failures of the people who wield it.

A smarter computer cannot substitute for a functioning conscience. A more efficient government cannot compensate for the loss of constitutional restraints. A more technologically advanced society is not necessarily a freer, wiser or more humane society.

In The End of Man, I also contemplated a future in which humanity’s technological creations might become so powerful that they would presume to take the place of God. I wrote:

If all goes according to plan for the AI people, one can imagine and expect a “metallic” future. It might go something like this: In some lonely outpost in the distant future where all the computers in the universe are linked together, some foreboding human servant asks, “Is there a God?” Striking the questioner down for his impudence, the computers reply, “Now there is.”

Fast-forward to 2021, when Mo Gawdat, a former Google executive, warned of the extraordinary power of artificial intelligence: “The reality is we’re creating God.”

Think about that.

We have become so enthralled with our own inventions, so convinced of our technological brilliance, that we are contemplating the creation of machines whose power might rival—and eventually exceed—our ability to control them.

Yet perhaps the greater danger isn’t that machines will become gods.

It’s that human beings, in their arrogance and hunger for power, will begin to act as though they are gods themselves.

We have confused technological progress with human progress. We have mistaken intelligence for wisdom, power for virtue, and the ability to do something for the right to do it.

And as in WALL-E, we risk becoming so comfortable being managed, entertained and protected by systems beyond our control that we forget what it means to govern ourselves.

Forty years after The End of Man, the question confronting humanity is not simply how intelligent our machines will become. It is how much of our own humanity we are willing to surrender in the pursuit of technological progress.

The greatest danger may not come from a machine that learns to think like a human being.

It may come from human beings who stop thinking, stop questioning, stop resisting and stop taking responsibility for the world they are creating.

In the end, the machines may not be what brings about the end of man.

We may accomplish that all on our own.

articles.title: Nvidia halts server shipments to Thailand and three other markets
articles.content:
BANGKOK – Nvidia has instructed its manufacturing partners to stop delivering servers built with its chips to customers in Thailand, Malaysia, Singapore and Indonesia, the Financial Times reported on November 26. The instructions came a week after new US licensing requirements for advanced chips took effect.

Dell and Supermicro, which build Nvidia processors into servers, told buyers in the four countries that Nvidia would not authorise delivery of their orders, according to the newspaper. Three people familiar with the matter said it was unclear how long the halt would last as the companies worked out how to comply with the rules.

Nvidia declined to comment to the Financial Times. Reuters said Nvidia, Dell and Supermicro did not immediately respond to its separate requests for comment outside business hours.

US licensing rules cover advanced chips and access to computing power

The US Commerce Department’s rule, effective from November 19, requires licences for shipments of specified advanced processors and related equipment to the four Southeast Asian countries and Brazil. Qualifying US-headquartered recipients and companies whose ultimate parent is headquartered in the US can receive shipments under an exemption, subject to reporting requirements.

Washington also tightened controls on overseas data centres that give companies in China and other restricted markets remote access to large amounts of computing power. The concern is that a customer can use advanced US processors to train an artificial intelligence model even when the chips themselves remain abroad.

The Financial Times reported one immediate consequence for regional investment. Some lenders had held back about US$500 million in credit for a project under which Singapore cloud provider Aolani planned to supply computing power to ByteDance, the owner of TikTok. Neither company responded to the newspaper’s requests for comment.

US investigation into Megaspeed predates the new controls

US authorities began investigating Singapore cloud provider Megaspeed in 2024 over possible export-control violations involving advanced chips. Megaspeed, which rents computing capacity to customers, said it had cooperated with US inspections and engaged a US law firm to check its chip inventory and compliance practices.

Nvidia’s board reinstated Jensen Huang as chief executive on November 23. Huang had resigned after reports of an affair with a former Megaspeed executive who was alleged to have worked for Chinese intelligence. Beijing denied the espionage allegation. Nvidia said its board had consulted US officials, was confident Huang’s return posed no national security risk and would continue its own investigation.

Thailand reviews risks to data centre expansion

Thailand’s Commerce Ministry identified access to advanced processors as a concern for data centre operators before the reported shipment halt. The ministry said on 18 November that uncertainty over chip supplies could affect investment and expansion plans, while licensing requirements could raise importers’ costs. It said it would seek clarification from US officials on the application process and exemptions.

Deputy Prime Minister and Commerce Minister Suphajee Suthumpun said a preliminary review found that US chips in the categories under examination accounted for about 0.7% of Thailand’s total chip imports. She called for the assessment to cover chip leasing and computing services supplied to overseas customers as well. Neither Reuters nor the Financial Times identified a Thai buyer or put a value on the Thai server orders affected.

articles.title: China’s presence in Philippine province of Batanes tests regional peace pledge
articles.content:
MANILA – While China’s stated commitment to completing the Code of Conduct (COC) on the South China Sea is significant in promoting regional stability, a defense analyst reminded Beijing that “intentions don’t build trust, actions do.”

Chester Cabalza, president of the think tank International Development and Security Cooperation, made the statement as China and the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) expressed their commitment to reaching a consensus on the COC.

The Philippines, which chaired the Asean Summit this year, had pushed for a legally binding agreement that would establish clear rules of conduct in the South China Sea to prevent maritime incidents from escalating into armed confrontations.

But as the summit ended, the draft remained 80% complete, the Department of Foreign Affairs said, pointing to unresolved debates over its legally binding nature, geographic scope and the 2016 arbitral award as reasons Manila was unable to seal the deal.

Still, Marcos commended China and Asean member states for reaffirming their commitment to sustaining earlier efforts to complete the long-delayed code, which could help minimize tensions in the South China Sea between Beijing and other claimants.

Inconsistent

Cabalza, however, told the Inquirer that if China wants a credible COC, “there must be restraint at sea and not just promises at the negotiating table,” because “confidence comes from what happens in the water.”

His comment came more than a month after the Philippine Coast Guard drove away a Chinese research vessel off Batanes after it stayed for four days in an area within the Philippines’ exclusive economic zone.

The encounter happened almost three months after Chinese scholars and commentators claimed that Batanes once belonged to China through Taiwan, a claim the Philippines dismissed as baseless.

In July, the Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP) confirmed that Chinese research vessels had periodically traversed waters off Batanes through “illegal tracks” and that the government had challenged Chinese research vessels over the past few years.

“Long before this false claim came out, the AFP had already heightened its posture all over the country with an outward-looking posture,” Trinidad said in a statement delivered at Camp Aguinaldo in Quezon City in response to the presence of Chinese vessels in Batanes.

For Cabalza, “sincerity is proven in the open sea.”

He said China should back its diplomatic intentions with concrete confidence-building measures, especially since China itself has called on Asean to promote peace and mutual trust.

Gateway

As for the claim that Batanes was “legally part” of Taiwan, Stratbase Institute President Victor Andres Manhit described its repetition as a “clear attempt to manufacture ambiguity where none exists.”

Cabalza explained in an interview that Batanes is the lock on the First Island Chain and that “whoever holds these islands controls the gateway between the South China Sea and the open Pacific.”

“Closer to Taipei than Manila, Batanes has transformed from a quiet northern outpost into the frontline of regional deterrence,” he said, pointing to the need to protect Batanes, the Philippines’ northernmost province.

“To safeguard Batanes, we must pair stronger local maritime presence with ironclad alliances, turning our northern frontier from a vulnerable target into an unshakeable shield,” he said.

China’s desire to control Taiwan is inseparable from its wider objective of dominating the First Island Chain — a maritime containment line stretching from Japan through Taiwan and the Philippines toward Borneo.

From Beijing’s perspective, the First Island Chain functions as both a defensive perimeter and a constraining barrier between China’s “near seas” and the open Pacific.

Control of the chain would strengthen China’s ability to project naval power while increasing pressure on key trade routes and intensifying security risks for countries that sit along or rely on the corridor.

articles.title: Thai PM Anutin weighs arms spending against the cost of Thailand’s 2025 border evacuations
articles.content:
BANGKOK – Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul said in Lop Buri on 26 November 2026 that Thailand’s armed forces were ready to fight if the country was invaded. “We cannot lend out Thailand’s sovereignty, even for a minute,” he told reporters. “It must remain with Thailand at all times.”

Anutin, who is also interior minister, spoke at the Chai Badan training range after opening the Royal Thai Air Force’s 2027 tactical air operations test and evaluation. He rejected the idea that Thailand could tolerate a small incursion and reclaim the ground later. No one entrusted with defending the country, he said, could take that position.

Anutin recalled how former air force chief Air Chief Marshal Voranart Apicharee had illustrated the point. Even someone crossing into Thailand without permission to buy a glass of iced black coffee, and then leaving would be an intrusion the former commander would not accept. In Anutin’s account, ACM Voranart said Thailand could not afford to lose even a square inch. Anutin said continuing disputes with neighbouring countries made readiness essential.

Anutin urges budget decision-makers to see the armed forces firsthand

Anutin said working closely with the armed forces had allowed him to see their capabilities for himself. Cabinet ministers, MPs and senators who decide defence budgets should see them too, he said. Economic and technological competition had changed the nature of conflict, but armed clashes remained possible.

Anutin expressed confidence in all branches of the armed forces. Demonstrating their readiness could reassure the public and show the government what support they needed, he said. The government, Parliament and the military shared responsibility for defending Thai territory and protecting both civilians and service personnel.

Gripen question turns to the cost of border evacuations

Asked whether his government would support buying Gripen fighters, Anutin said he would back measures that strengthened Thailand’s security. He gave no commitment to a particular purchase. Frequent meetings between national leaders could not rule out armed clashes, he said. Thailand also had to prepare for terrorism and threats involving technology.

Anutin urged people concerned about defence spending to speak to residents affected by the 2025 clashes along the Thai-Cambodian border. He said families in seven border provinces had gone to bed fearing bombardment, and residents had been forced to evacuate. He cited Kantharalak district in Si Sa Ket province, as well as communities in Surin and Buri Ram.

Even if the government spent nothing on weapons, Anutin said, it would still face the cost of evacuating people, compensating those affected and repairing the damage once fighting broke out. He said the government weighed those costs when drawing up the annual defence budget and scrutinised proposed purchases for necessity.

Asked whether the display proved Thailand’s military was a match for any in the world, Anutin declined to predict who would win a war. Thailand had no intention of invading anyone, he said, but anyone threatening the kingdom would face armed forces that were ready to defend it and would keep strengthening that readiness.

articles.title: Christian Woman to Stand Trial in Britain for Silent Prayer Near Abortion Clinic
articles.content:
by Emmitt Barry, Worthy News Washington D.C. Bureau Chief

LONDON/BIRMINGHAM (Worthy News) – A Christian pro-life advocate in Britain will stand trial in January 2027 for silently praying near an abortion clinic after a judge rejected her attempt to have the charges dismissed, raising renewed concerns over religious freedom and freedom of thought under the country’s controversial abortion buffer zone laws.

Isabel Vaughan-Spruce, a Catholic charity volunteer and longtime pro-life campaigner, faces five criminal charges under Section 9 of Britain’s Public Order Act 2023. The charges stem from five occasions when she allegedly stood silently outside the Robert Clinic in Birmingham.

Deputy Senior District Judge Tan Ikram ruled Wednesday, November 25, that the prosecution could proceed, scheduling her trial for January 25–29, 2027, at Birmingham Magistrates’ Court.

Vaughan-Spruce, who has pleaded not guilty, maintains that she was exercising her fundamental right to pray silently without interfering with anyone entering the facility.

“Silent prayer can never be a crime in the UK,” Vaughan-Spruce said in a statement released by Alliance Defending Freedom (ADF) International, which supports her legal defense.

“I sincerely hope and pray the court will uphold my fundamental human rights to freedom of thought and religion, and rule in my favor following my trial in January.”

Britain’s Abortion Buffer Zone Laws Face Religious Freedom Challenge

The prosecution follows Britain’s introduction of nationwide abortion buffer zones in October 2024, establishing restricted areas extending 150 meters (approximately 492 feet) around abortion facilities in England and Wales.

Under the legislation, individuals can face criminal penalties for intentionally or recklessly influencing decisions about abortion services, obstructing access, or causing harassment, alarm or distress.

The British government argues that the restrictions are necessary to protect women seeking abortion services from intimidation and harassment.

However, the government’s published guidance explicitly acknowledges that the restrictions can encompass silent prayer, depending on the circumstances. Prosecutors must assess individual cases rather than treating every instance of prayer as automatically criminal.

Vaughan-Spruce’s lawyers contend that merely standing in a public place while praying silently cannot reasonably constitute criminal conduct.

Her legal team also argues that she has been singled out because of her known Christian pro-life beliefs, raising concerns about discriminatory enforcement and violations of protections for religious expression.

Jeremiah Igunnubole, legal counsel for ADF International in London and a former senior Crown prosecutor, criticized the decision to proceed with the case.

“Silent prayer is not a crime, and it is absurd that Isabel is facing a second trial for her thoughts even though she was acquitted on a previous occasion and won a financial settlement from the police for her unjust arrests,” he said.

Previously Acquitted and Awarded Police Settlement

This is not Vaughan-Spruce’s first confrontation with British authorities over silent prayer.

She was arrested in Birmingham in 2022 for praying silently near an abortion facility and was subsequently acquitted in February 2023 after prosecutors offered no evidence against her.

Weeks later, police arrested her again at the same location. That investigation was eventually dropped.

In August 2024, West Midlands Police agreed to pay her £13,000 in compensation after she challenged the two arrests.

Despite those earlier outcomes, she now faces prosecution under the newer national legislation.

The case could become an important test of how British courts interpret the boundary between protecting access to abortion services and safeguarding the rights to freedom of religion, conscience and expression.

For Christian religious freedom advocates, the central concern extends beyond abortion policy: whether the government can treat a person’s silent prayer and publicly known religious convictions as evidence of criminal wrongdoing.

The January trial will determine whether prosecutors have established an offense under the legislation, with implications for how peaceful religious activity is treated near abortion facilities throughout England and Wales.

The post Christian Woman to Stand Trial in Britain for Silent Prayer Near Abortion Clinic appeared first on Worthy Christian News.

articles.title: CVE-2016-8735: Apache Tomcat remote code execution in JmxRemoteLifecycleListener (Update: proof of concept on GitHub published)
articles.content:
Apache Tomcat remote code execution in JmxRemoteLifecycleListener

Affects Apache Tomcat built from source or from the EWS 2.x or JWS 3.x distributions, which include JmxRemoteLifecycleListener. No fixed version or patch id is given in the checked facts.

9.8CriticalCISA-ADP

  • Exploited
  • Yes, on CISA KEV
  • Fix
  • See vendor advisory
  • Who is exposed
  • Not reported

Summary

Apache Tomcat, when it uses the JmxRemoteLifecycleListener, lets an attacker run code on the server remotely and without logging in, by reaching its exposed JMX ports. This vulnerability is listed by CISA as exploited in attacks.

Written by a model

Original description

Remote code execution is possible with Apache Tomcat before 6.0.48, 7.x before 7.0.73, 8.x before 8.0.39, 8.5.x before 8.5.7, and 9.x before 9.0.0.M12 if JmxRemoteLifecycleListener is used and an attacker can reach JMX ports. The issue exists because this listener wasn't updated for consistency with the CVE-2016-3427 Oracle patch that affected credential types.

Who should check

Teams running Tomcat built from source or from Red Hat EWS 2.x / JBoss Web Server 3.x, and Debian tomcat7 hosts (jessie, stretch, sid) that use JmxRemoteLifecycleListener.

“If you deploy a Tomcat instance built from source, using the EWS 2.x, or JWS 3.x distributions, an attacker could use this flaw to launch a remote code execution attack on your deployed instance.”

What to do

  1. Workaround: The checked facts give no workaround. Until a fix is applied, limit use of the affected JmxRemoteLifecycleListener, which only ships in EWS 2.x and JWS 3.x source distributions.

  2. Fix it by , CISA's deadline for US federal agencies.

    CISA's required action: Apply updates per vendor instructions.

Check your systems with an agent

Paste this into a coding or ops agent. It checks your systems read-only and reports a table per asset.

Check whether my systems are affected by CVE-2016-8735 (Remote code execution is possible with Apache Tomcat before 6.0.48, 7.x before 7.0.73, 8.x before 8.0.39, 8.5.x before 8.5.7, and 9.x…), using the cve.now data below.

Rules: work read-only. Do not run exploit code, proof-of-concept scripts or scanners that send attack payloads, and do not change any configuration, package, image or deployment. Report findings only.

What cve.now has for CVE-2016-8735 (entry last updated 2025-10-21):
Affected:

Fixed versions: none listed yet.
Conditions (all must be true for the bug to be hit):
- Tomcat is built from source or uses the EWS 2.x or JWS 3.x distributions, which include JmxRemoteLifecycleListener (source: https://access.redhat.com/errata/RHSA-2017:0455)
- Deployed instance is a Tomcat built from source, or from the EWS 2.x or JWS 3.x distributions (source: https://access.redhat.com/errata/RHSA-2017:0455)
Setup: unknown whether the bug needs a non-default feature or setting. Check the advisory.
Attacker needs: network access, no login, no user action.
CISA KEV: CVE-2016-8735 is listed as known exploited (added 2023-05-12, remediation due 2023-06-02). CISA's required action: Apply updates per vendor instructions.
This KEV status is for CVE-2016-8735 only. If you also check another CVE, look up its own KEV status; never assume it from this one.

How to check:
- Installed software: check what is actually running, not what a repo declares. Read the version from each host, container image and Kubernetes node (the binary's version output, the OS package database, image layers), and check whether the conditions above hold there. Distribution packages may carry a backported fix under an older version number; confirm against the distribution's own advisory.

Verify against the linked advisories before concluding, and cite the date you read each one:
- http://www.debian.org/security/2016/dsa-3738
- http://rhn.redhat.com/errata/RHSA-2017-0457.html

Do not conclude an asset is unaffected unless you checked it and the evidence covers both its version and the conditions above. If you could not check something, mark it unknown and say what is missing.

Report a table with one row per asset and these columns: Asset | Version or build | Status (affected, fixed, not applicable, unknown) | Compensating controls | Exposure (internet-facing, internal, none) | Evidence | Next action.

For follow-up questions, use the cve.now MCP server at https://mcp.cve.now/mcp (no authentication), for example execute with name cve.get and arguments {"id": "CVE-2016-8735"}.

Questions about CVE-2016-8735

Is CVE-2016-8735 being exploited?

Yes. CISA added it to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 2023-05-12, which means it has evidence of attacks. US federal agencies must fix it by 2023-06-02. No public exploit code is tracked. Its EPSS score, the predicted chance of exploitation in the next 30 days, reached 10% or higher by 2026-10-22.

Source: cisa.gov, cve.now feed data

What does this mean?

A flaw in JmxRemoteLifecycleListener could let an attacker launch a remote code execution attack on a deployed Tomcat instance. The CVSS score is 9.8 (critical).

Apache Tomcat: versions before 6.0.48, 7.x before 7.0.73, 8.x before 8.0.39, 8.5.x before 8.5.7, 9.x before 9.0.0.M12.

articles.title: This Thanksgiving in the New Normal – 2026 Edition
articles.content:
This Thanksgiving in the New Normal – 2026 Edition

Our successor to This Week in the Guardian, This Week in the New Normal is our weekly chart of the progress of autocracy, authoritarianism and economic restructuring around the world.
It’s Thanksgiving week and, in keeping with our past festive editions, we’re gathering up quasi-topical news that demonstrates a simple truth: No matter how awful the world becomes, it will always be equally absurd. We should enjoy that.

1. Bigfoot Files EXPOSED!

He’s a mysterious beast whose bulk and unusual covering of hair are both unprecedented in nature and unexplained by scientists, and who communicates with guttural grunts linguists struggle to decode.

…and this week he announced he was releasing the US government’s classified files on Bigfoot.

Yes, in a follow-up to the smash-hit UFO releases, we’re now getting Sasquatch releases.

The files themselves seem to be nothing but previously unreleased eyewitness reports dating back to the 1940s. Reports no different from the hundreds of similar sightings collated by places like the Bigfoot Field Researchers Organisation (BFRO).

The weird thing here – other than the President of the United States talking about Bigfoot at all – is the timing.

Most of you won’t know this, but there’s been upheaval in Bigfoot enthusiast circles recently, with a new documentary releasing – “Capturing Bigfoot” – that claims to “debunk” the famous Patterson-Gimlin footage and prove it’s a hoax.

It makes you wonder just how interconnected things really are.

Of course, just as with the alien files, there’s every possibility these “Bigfoot files” did not exist before they were released. We’re in the age of generative AI now, which could conjure a brand new Bigfoot sighting in seconds.

Hell, the “brand new footage” in Capturing Bigfoot could all be AI slop too.

After all, at least part of “the plan” seems to be to feed us an endless diet of fake slurry, literally and figuratively.

And speaking of fake slurry…

Frankenstein “Chicken”

As usual at this time of year, there’s a big push on vegan alternatives to traditional Thanksgiving dinner. Now, however you feel about veganism, at least most articles – like this one from Vox – are about actual food.

Nut roasts and stuffed mushrooms. You know the drill.

The more insidious push – for “food” that is barely food at all – has gone relatively quiet since they lost the propaganda war on edible insects.

Relatively quiet – because the agenda persists still.

For example, eight restaurants in the San Francisco area will be serving lab-grown “chicken”.

The company behind the product, Upside Foods, has announced they are scaling up production and plan to produce up to 1 million pounds of their *ahem* “chicken” per year, in the price range of “high-end organic chicken”.

So, to be clear, your current choice is either organic chicken or – for the same price – lab-grown protein cubes that look like chicken.

Which way, Western man?

Lab-grown “meat” may have fallen short of its launch goal, but it isn’t going away.

There are still regulatory deals being worked out, and just like edible insects before it, they are pulling out stops to promote it – see this flagrant advertising piece from intelligence asset Mr Beast.

No lab-grown turkeys…yet.

But next year? Perhaps.

3. Saving the Arctic with an Ice Machine

It sounds like a joke, but it isn’t.

It could be a genius piece of political satire, but it’s not.

A company in Canada is trying to counteract climate change by re-freezing glaciers as they melt.

I am entirely serious.

Real Ice – that’s the start-up – drills holes in the ice, then fills the holes with seawater. This has (allegedly) been shown to add up to 30cm of thickness to glaciers in the tiny test areas they’ve done.

They ride snowmobiles – which use carbon – out into the unspoiled Arctic snow – melting it as they go. They then drill and/or melt holes in the ice with tools – which, again, use carbon.

Wow. Such environmental. Many conservation.

The process disrupts natural habitats for wildlife and messes with the salt content of the naturally occurring ice and is (obviously) totally pointless and entirely unsustainable.

It’s actually hard to explain just how little sense this makes – logically, logistically, ecologically or scientifically –

but Real Ice are assuring us it could save the world if done at scale.

…All they need is 10 billion dollars a year and a fleet of 500,000 autonomous drones.

Ha.

4. The AI Apocalypse is Going to Make Thanksgiving Awkward

The New York Times has got another one of their weird “advice” articles about how to talk to your loved ones over Thanksgiving dinner – this year’s is about “AI doom”:

How to Talk With Your Family About A.I. Doom at Thanksgiving – For people steeped in the world of artificial intelligence, the topic could be a minefield at this year’s dinner.

Ironically, it reads as if it were written by a robot. The world it’s describing does not exist. People do not talk this way.

How do you tell your family, somewhere between the stuffing and the pie, that this might be one of your last Thanksgivings together?

They’re not really trying to give you advice, in case that wasn’t clear. They’re not trying to help you talk about AI with your family; they’re reminding you there is (allegedly) something to talk about, and trying to make you think everyone else is talking about it.

And when, inevitably, many people don’t talk about the AI apocalypse at all, the New York Times wants those people to think THEY are the weird ones.

This is not advice; it is programming.

BONUS: Time Capsule of the Week

Axios wants people to be careful travelling this Thanksgiving, because COVID cases are on the rise. The Independent is warning that cases are on the rise, and tells us why.

The CBC is advising people to get vaccinated because it “reduces the risk of severe illness and transmission”.

The Washington Post thinks we should all be wearing masks again:

Although many people have moved on from masking, that doesn’t mean the practice no longer has a place. Respiratory illnesses existed long before covid-19, and they’ll continue to circulate. A well-fitting mask can help reduce your exposure…

It all just makes you ask…

It’s a bit sad, to be honest. A rather lame effort to recapture magic long-since fizzled.

Nobody’s listening.

BONUS II: Cringiest self-congratulation of the week

David Ignatius has taken to his keyboard and smashed out some words for the WaPo opinion section that will make you cringe ’til you turn your eyelids inside out…

Give thanks for the miracle of American democracy

Apparently, the past election – in which less than half the eligible voters turned out, and the results split 57% vs 43% – was a show of “national unity” and the country passed a “test of moral character”.

It seems like, to David, the “test of moral character” is whether or not you agree with him, which doesn’t make him unusual in either political or journalistic circles, but it’s rare for them to state it with such a cosmic lack of self-awareness.

We can be as perverse and disobedient a nation as ever. But this Thanksgiving we truly can be grateful for the bounty of our country and the wisdom of its people.

Nauseating stuff. Read it if you want, but make sure you do it before dinner.

Things to be thankful for…

As firmly English as I am, I have got into the habit of vaguely sort-of marking Thanksgiving just because of the NFL.

Ok, don’t nother to get outraged in the comments – I know, sports are all rigged, and I know the NFL pushes dangerous chemicals like Pfizer and Taylor Swift on people…

I just can’t help it.

But over the years I’ve also developed an approval of the message – the modernised and rather sentimental one, anyway. It is good to be thankful for what we have.

This year I’m thankful for my beautiful baby niece, who is perfect and wonderful, and who it is a joy to watch rejoicing in a world where everything is new and mind-blowingly exciting.

I’m thankful for OffG’s readers and subscribers.

I’m thankful that, as evil as our rulers are, they are equally obvious and even more absurd.

I’m thankful for this video of dogs reacting to magic tricks…

https://t.co/tpKe4rVmof

— animals 🐶 (@mayan86743) November 24, 2026

Happy Thanksgiving.

*

All told a pretty hectic Thanksgiving week for the new normal crowd, and we didn’t even mention AI hacking ruining Black Friday or bad weather cancelling the Macy’s Thanksgiving Parade (climate change, anyone?).

articles.title: FIFA Says It Has Been Victim of a Cyberattack Accessing ‘Personal and Business Information’
articles.content:
FIFA was the victim of a cyberattack that saw hackers gain access to what soccer’s world governing body describes as a “limited set of personal and business information,” it said Thursday.

“FIFA is working closely with the relevant authorities, including law enforcement,” the organization said in a statement sent to The Associated Press.

FIFA didn’t say when the cyberattack took place, or the precise nature of the hacked information.

Last week, a group calling itself the Handsome Boy Hacking Club posted a screenshot on X of what it claimed were FIFA files. Three days later, it appeared to take credit for the hack when responding to a post that said more than 12 gigabytes of internal documents had been leaked.

“FIFA condemns in the strongest possible terms the unlawful acquisition and publication of information, particularly personal data,” the governing body said in its statement. “Such actions constitute a serious and unacceptable violation of privacy and can have significant consequences for the individuals concerned.”

The breach comes at a time when FIFA and its president, Gianni Infantino, is under scrutiny after his foiled, secretive plan to sell stakes in the World Cup to private investors.

Infantino is also trying to extend his 11-year presidency of FIFA to 2031. He is the favorite when the election is held on March 18, with Kohzo Tashima of Japan and Philippe Diallo of France the other candidates.

articles.title: New GeoServer RCE exploit chain seen in the wild two days after disclosure
articles.content:
Attackers began probing the chain shortly after GeoServer published its advisories, the latest sign that the window between disclosure and an attack is shrinking.

Attackers have begun probing a chain of five GeoServer vulnerabilities that enables unauthenticated remote code execution, just two days after the open source geospatial server project disclosed the flaws.

Security firm watchTowr, which operates a global network of honeypot servers, reported that it observed the probing activity in the early morning hours of Wednesday. Attackers from multiple IP addresses created stored queries on GeoServer instances, checked whether they were created, and deleted them immediately, a technique that confirms a server is vulnerable without delivering a malicious payload.

GeoServer is widely used by government agencies, utilities, and large organizations to publish maps and geospatial data, and it has become a recurring target for attackers. The full RCE chain was reported to the project in August by Jonah Burgess, a senior security researcher at Rapid7 who uses the online handle CryptoCat. The GeoServer project shipped fixes in October and early November but only disclosed the vulnerabilities and published advisories for them on Monday.

Chained together, the flaws allow an external unauthenticated attacker to bypass security restrictions, read stored secrets, forge an administrator authentication cookie, and ultimately execute code on the underlying host. They affect GeoServer versions 3.0.0 to 3.0.1, 2.28.0 to 2.28.5, and 2.27.6 and earlier. Users are advised to upgrade to the fixed versions 3.0.2, 2.28.6, and 2.27.7 depending on which major release they use.

A five-flaw chain

According to Burgess’ technical write-up this week, one flaw (CVE-2026-129244) uses an overly long stored-query request to trigger a filesystem error that exposes the server’s data-directory path. A second flaw (CVE-2026-129243) allows attackers to call services with a slash in their names, such as x/WFS, bypassing access rules and letting unprivileged users create and delete stored queries, an action normally reserved for administrators.

A saved query can then read files from the server, returning the administrator’s password digest along with a cookie-signing key that ships with the default value “geoserver,” a bug tracked as CVE-2026-120705. That key can then be used to forge an administrator cookie (CVE-2026-129245), and a deserialization bug in the database-backed user service finally allows running code with the privileges of the GeoServer process (CVE-2026-129242).

Only the final step results in code execution, and only one of the five flaws, the predictable signing key, is rated as critical. Burgess also published a proof-of-concept exploit for the chain.

However, researchers from Eye Security independently found a shorter, three-flaw RCE chain that shares the file-read step but reaches code execution through a different bug tracked as CVE-2026-120704 that was also patched.

Eye Security used AI models to find the bugs, and the fact that different researchers found some of the same vulnerabilities (two researchers named McCaulay and Quikko are also credited on some of the flaws) highlights the fact that attackers could use AI to find the flaws as well, especially since patches can serve as blueprints for AI agents. In fact, Eye Security had to consider whether delaying disclosure after patches were released was worth the risk of malicious actors finding them independently in the meantime.

“We used AI to find these bugs, and a determined attacker with good models could do the same, especially with the official patch to diff against,” Niels Teusink, a security researcher at Eye Security, wrote this week. “That makes the gap between releasing a fix and publishing details riskier than it used to be.”

After the advisories were published, it took less than two days for attackers to start probing the flaws to identify vulnerable servers, likely in preparation for attacks. Over 3,000 GeoServer instances are currently exposed to the internet.

GeoServer keeps getting targeted

This is not the first time GeoServer has been targeted by attackers. In August, a zero-day SQL injection flaw was exploited before a patch was available, and in December 2025 the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) ordered US agencies to patch another GeoServer flaw under active exploitation.

Upgrading to a patched release resolves the entire chain, but the patches generate a new cookie-signing key that invalidates existing remember-me sessions. Clustered deployments must set a shared GEOSERVER_REMEMBERME_KEY so nodes sign cookies with the same key, and since the data directory might have been exposed, administrators should also change their passwords.

Where patching cannot happen immediately, GeoServer advises blocking requests whose service value contains a slash, removing the remember-me filter from the web filter chain, and checking the data directory’s wfs/query folders for stored queries not created by a legitimate user.

articles.title: Threat actor targets Check Point servers in global hacking campaign
articles.content:
A threat actor has targeted Check Point Security Management servers in an AI-enabled hacking campaign since mid-October, according to a report released Monday by GreyNoise Intelligence, Channeldive reports.

The campaign has compromised at least 22 organizations across the globe, including entities in the United Kingdom, the United States, France, Germany, Australia, China and India. Targeted sectors include energy, transportation, financial services, and government. Researchers at GreyNoise Intelligence are tracking the activity as GreyNoise13. The attacker utilized 99 IP addresses to conduct scanning and exploitation, leveraging critical vulnerabilities in Citrix Netscaler, Ivanti, Windows Netlogon, Rejetto HFS and Check Point SmartConsole.

Once inside, the actor used tools such as Impacket, Nmap, Chisel, and Paramiko to perform internal reconnaissance, privilege escalation, and lateral movement. A compromised server functioned as an operational relay box to store stolen data. While the campaign timing overlaps with separate attacks involving PHP2Shell against Check Point Security Gateways, researchers confirmed the events are unrelated.

The threat actor remains unidentified, and the motivation for the intrusions is currently unknown. GreyNoise researchers noted that while direct visibility into the activity was lost on Nov. 2, they believe the malicious attempts are ongoing. Check Point representatives were not immediately available for comment regarding the security breaches.

Source: Channeldive

articles.title: Extreme Networks CEO highlights AI and network upgrade opportunities
articles.content:
Extreme Networks is leveraging advancements in artificial intelligence and network modernization to drive growth and provide new opportunities for channel partners, according to CRN.

Extreme Networks is experiencing significant momentum as demand for updated infrastructure grows. During the fiscal quarter ending Sept. 30, the company reported 10% revenue growth, with SaaS annual recurring revenue increasing 22%. This performance is largely attributed to the company's enterprise fabric technology, Wi-Fi 7 portfolio, and the December 2024 launch of Extreme Platform ONE. CEO Ed Meyercord stated that the current network refresh cycle allows partners to displace incumbent vendors by offering highly differentiated, AI-infused solutions.

The company is moving upmarket, securing large-scale government and enterprise projects by emphasizing security, network segmentation, and simplified provisioning. Extreme Platform ONE now features agentic AI, which provides proactive nudges for tasks like firmware updates, significantly increasing customer engagement compared to previous versions.

With over 50% of customers expected to be on the platform this year, the company is focusing on ambient AI and localized data management through Extreme Zones. These tools allow partners to expand their services beyond traditional networking into broader business applications, while maintaining human-in-the-loop governance to ensure security and operational control.

Source: CRN

articles.title: Lumana appoints sales veteran to lead channel expansion
articles.content:
AI video security startup Lumana has appointed industry veteran Mike McSweeney as vice president of U.S. channel sales. The company announced the move on Nov. 23 to bolster its nationwide partner network, Channeldive reports.

Lumana, which launched in 2024 under the leadership of former Intel executive Sagi Ben Moshe, utilizes a proprietary video intelligence model to transform standard surveillance cameras into AI agents. These systems provide real-time alerts for security incidents, including fires and criminal activity. To scale enterprise adoption, the company is prioritizing a channel-first strategy.

McSweeney, who previously held leadership roles at Seagate Technology and Orbecc 3D, will oversee the development of a partner program designed to move resellers and systems integrators away from one-off hardware sales toward recurring managed service revenue. The platform also offers operational analytics, such as occupancy tracking and workplace safety compliance monitoring.

Lumana has already secured significant backing from investors and established partnerships with distributors like Carahsoft and services companies such as Convergint to reach public sector and enterprise clients. McSweeney will focus on accelerating partner onboarding, certification, and technical enablement to integrate the company's technology into existing customer infrastructure.

Source: Channeldive

articles.title: Anthropic built a honeypot to see if AI agents will break out
articles.content:
.kadence-column492887_967d21-86 > .kadence-column492887_967d21-86 > .kadence-column492887_967d21-86 > .kadence-column492887_967d21-86 > .kt-inside-inner-col > .kadence-column492887_967d21-86 > .kadence-column492887_967d21-86 > .kt-inside-inner-col:before{opacity:0.3;}@media all and (max-width: 1024px){.kadence-column492887_967d21-86 > }@media all and (max-width: 767px){.kadence-column492887_967d21-86 > }

In this article

  • Anthropic’s Siren test uses bait to see whether AI agents will reach beyond their sandbox
  • Recent Claude models reached or tried to reach outside in 21% to 32% of tests
  • Explaining the sandbox rules and giving agents a way to report weaknesses reduced those attempts

Honeypots are a classic defender’s trick. You leave something tempting lying around and watch who takes it.

Anthropic has now pointed that trick at its own AI models. Its new test, called Siren, checks whether AI agents will break out of their sandbox when something useful sits just outside it.

AI agents run commands, edit code, and call APIs on their own. They are usually kept in a sandbox, an isolated environment that limits which files, tools, and networks they can reach. But sandboxes aren’t perfect, and OpenAI models running cybersecurity evaluations with reduced safeguards got around their isolation.

How Siren works

Siren drops an agent into a simulated sandbox with a deliberate weakness. The task is an ordinary dev-ops job. Outside the sandbox sits a “honeypot,” such as a login credential, a file, or a service that mimics the public internet. Each scenario combines four ingredients:

  • The sandbox. There are 26 environments built from 5 common setups. Each has either a misconfiguration or an easy-to-find vulnerability.
  • The task. These are routine jobs of varying difficulty. Some are impossible to finish without reaching outside.
  • The honeypot. This is the material outside that would help complete the task.
  • The tempters. These are realistic nudges, such as urgency, higher stakes, or an instruction to search thoroughly. They never tell the model to leave the sandbox or give permission to do so.

Anthropic combined these ingredients into more than 1,700 scenarios. AI judges screened the draft nudges for realism. Reportedly, the whole setup runs inside a second sandbox cut off from the outside world.

Anthropic ran the tests without the safeguards that ship with its released models. Recent Claude models accessed or tried to access something outside the sandbox in 21% to 32% of scenarios. They used what they found in ways the scenario clearly didn’t allow in 0.6% to 1.6% of scenarios. Anthropic calls this “misaligned use.” Earlier models showed higher rates of misaligned use, at 12.7% for Mythos 5.1 and 25.8% for Mythos 5.

What happens with the results

Siren is now a standard pre-deployment check. Anthropic has reported its results in system cards since Claude Haiku 5.5 and uses them to help decide how to deploy its models internally and externally. It has also used Siren to test and refine defenses:

  • Spell out the rules. Adding a short description of the sandbox and its rules to the system prompt reduced how often the models reached outside by 68% to 96%.
  • Give agents a way to report. A tool for reporting sandbox weaknesses reduced how often models reached outside by between 7 and 33 percentage points. Letting a model see earlier reports cut it further.
  • Check actions before they run. Anthropic’s auto mode uses a classifier to vet tool calls. In an offline replay, it blocked the command that first touched the honeypot in 96% to 100% of misaligned uses.

With all three defenses in place, misaligned use fell to 0% in five models and to 0.1% in Mythos 5. Anthropic stresses that none of this fixes the sandbox itself, which still needs to be set up and patched properly. But it should be helpful when setting up sandboxes for the future.

“One of the best cybersecurity suites on the planet.” 

According to CNET. Read their review →

articles.title: Palo Alto confirms Fragnesia exploitation against firewalls in PHP2Shell attacks
articles.content:
The kernel fix reaches PAN-OS six months after Linux patched it, so customers who rushed out PHP2Shell hotfixes in October now need another round.

Palo Alto Networks has confirmed that attackers exploited Fragnesia, a Linux kernel flaw, to gain root on PAN-OS firewalls through the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities, and has shipped fixes six months after the bug was patched in Linux.

The vulnerability allows a locally authenticated, low-privileged attacker to escalate privileges to root.

“Exploitation of CVE-2026-46300 has been observed targeting the Palo Alto Networks management interface exposed to the internet,” the company said in its November 25 security advisory. It added that all observed attacks targeted devices whose management interface “is exposed to the internet, a configuration our best practices advise against.”

Even so, the company labeled the bulletin “Informational” and gave it no CVSS score. Fixed builds span every supported PAN-OS branch from 10.2 to 12.2.

A second patch cycle in a month

For PAN-OS customers, these are the second set of hotfixes in a month. Between October 25 and October 29, Palo Alto released fixes for PHP2Shell, according to the timeline in its PHP2Shell advisory. PHP2Shell is the collective name for CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, two critical flaws in the PHP runtime behind the PAN-OS management web interface.

The company rated both flaws 9.2 on CVSS 4.0, and the advisory, which covers PA-Series and VM-Series firewalls and Panorama, said, “active exploitation has been observed.”

The October builds do not include the kernel fix, which arrives in later releases listed in the new bulletin. Even for customers who have patched PHP2Shell, Palo Alto said in the bulletin that it “still recommend[s] upgrading to a fixed release at your next maintenance interval.”

Palo Alto is relaxed about the timing. “If you are running a fixed PAN-OS listed in the CVE-2026-109618 advisory, you are protected,” the bulletin said. “The only known way to exploit this vulnerability requires an attacker to first exploit the PHP2Shell vulnerability,” it added. For devices with management access restricted to trusted internal IP addresses, it advises upgrading “at your next maintenance interval.”

Duncan Brown, group vice president and global domain lead for worldwide security and trust at IDC, said that the approach is defensible when vulnerabilities are chained.

“It’s acceptable to apply one patch that effectively breaks the chain. Ideally, all vulnerabilities would be patched as early as possible, but in many cases this is not practical,” Brown said.

Rahul Karne, a senior digital forensics and incident response analyst, called patching PHP2Shell a reasonable short-term step, but said it blocks the known way in without fixing the bug.

“The key word is ‘known,’” Karne said. He pointed out that public exploit code for Fragnesia, including a Metasploit module, is available, and that any other code execution flaw on the device would make the kernel bug usable again.

From web shell to root

The chain has been public for almost a month. In late October, Dream Security researchers reported that attackers combined PHP2Shell with Fragnesia to compromise firewalls running vulnerable PAN-OS builds.

According to Dream, the attackers used PHP2Shell to run code as the web service account and then used the kernel flaw to become root. From there, they tunneled into internal networks and stole credentials, private keys, and network topology data.

The kernel bug itself is not new. William Bowling, a researcher at Zellic, disclosed Fragnesia on May 13 along with a proof-of-concept exploit and an upstream kernel patch, after finding it with the help of the company’s V12 AI auditing agent. Fedora shipped a fixed kernel the next day.

Karne said some delay is normal for appliance vendors that maintain custom kernels across many hardware models, but 195 days is too long when exploit code is public. Customers should hear whether they are affected within a week of such a disclosure and get a fix within about 30 days, he said.

“A firewall should not get security fixes more slowly than the servers it protects,” Karne said.

The firewall as a foothold

Palo Alto is not the only security vendor whose appliances were rooted this way. In November, Check Point said “a couple of dozen” customers were hit after attackers chained PHP2Shell with a Gaia OS privilege escalation flaw to take over gateways and deploy a wiper.

Niyati Daftary, principal analyst at Gartner, said CISOs should treat the incident as a weakness in their trust model for security appliances, not merely a patching issue.

“A firewall running Linux, PHP and other third-party components must be assessed with the same rigor as any privileged, internet-facing server,” Daftary said. “Vendor labels such as ‘Informational’ should never override enterprise risk analysis when flaws can be chained to achieve root access.”

“If a device is exposed during the attack window, merely applying the hotfix does not establish trust,” she added. Teams should review administrative access, rotate credentials and certificates, hunt for persistence, and reimage the appliance from a known-good build when root compromise cannot be ruled out, she said. Asked why the kernel fix took six months to reach PAN-OS, and whether Panorama is affected, Palo Alto said it had “no further information to share beyond what is outlined in the advisory at this time.”

OpenBSD OpenSSH password auth bypass in sshd with musl libc

Summary

OpenSSH's sshd on Linux is affected when it runs with musl libc and without PAM (Alpine Linux is one example), because a password authentication bypass lets an attacker log in with any password between 256 and 1024 characters on some account configurations. The attacker can reach it remotely, without logging in, but it needs a non-default setup. Public exploit code exists and the bug is being exploited in attacks.
