articles.title: Why “AI Hacking” Will Make Tech Outages “The New Normal”
articles.content:
Why “AI Hacking” Will Make Tech Outages “The New Normal”

Last week, we posted an article highlighting all the (allegedly unrelated) tech outages that had afflicted Microsoft, Apple, the FAA, JP Morgan, Anthropic and the NSA.

Since then it’s just gone on and on.

Two days ago, the FBI’s crime database was allegedly hacked. And, for some reason, the FBI rushed to tell everybody about it.

Then the United States Department of Agriculture was hacked as well, with attackers allegedly targeting systems that made payments to farmers.

…and then America’s ports in general, as hackers are said to be disrupting “vital trade routes” with an “onslaught” of cyber attacks.

…and then their warships.

…and then a city in California, exposing under-cover police identities.

…and then the US Treasury’s financial crimes unit.

…and then the CIA itself, though allegedly only their “unclassified” data, and again – for some reason – they told everyone about it.

These were (allegedly) “hacks” this time, by the way. Not “temporary service delays” caused by “outdated hardware” or “internal maintenance”, which is what all the outages were officially blamed on last week.

A ransomware cyberattack blamed on hacking group “non” supposedly breached Chase, VISA and Mastercard’s systems, but – we’re told – this was totally separate from the online banking outage.

And this issue is no longer limited to the US either. You could argue it never was.

We’re less than a month removed from the “hacked” supermarket freezers destroying tons of food across seven countries.

The last week has seen Transport for London hacked, along with UK-based retailer NEXT, and wealth management firm St James’ Place.

Over the weekend, Norwegian government digital identity platform ID-porten was hit with a DDOS attack, and the Norwegian-based energy company Equinor – the largest gas supplier in Europe – got attacked.

Three days ago, the European Union announced it had been the victim of a cyber-attack last month, but never told anyone before.

Then, earlier today, the European Commission reported it was being subjected to another cyberattack, which took the European Academy offline.

Spanish football league La Liga was hit with a hack that exposed fan data, Bell Canada got hit with an “agentic attack” that exposed customer data, and Guadeloupe hospital’s IT systems were shut down after yet another cyber-attack.

Again, all reported over this past weekend.

The Indian press reports the Indian government’s Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) is warning that AI-assisted cyber attacks on banks and fintech firms are making unauthorised payments.

Just about an hour ago (at the time of writing), the Israeli police reported they had shut down their communication systems after they were hacked.

…the hacks just keep on coming.

Allegedly.

Because, we should remember, there’s no evidence most of these “attacks” happened as described, or even at all, it’s just a snowstorm of panic words with very little that can be described as substantive verification.

They may be made up in their entirety. Like so much else.

Or, as we saw with food warnings over the summer, they may be perfectly normal activity suddenly elevated to front pages to create the idea of a new problem simply by amplifying the routine.

OffG, for example, is constantly having little niggling hack attempts or DDoS attacks, and if we were to begin broadcasting the fact every time it happened, it would appear to be a spike in nefarious activity.

Clearly, the banking and Microsoft outages really happened, and clearly planes were really grounded…but even here we don’t know how, or why.

Whatever the nature of the chaos-induction, it has has resulted in the US Cyber-Security Commissioner Sean Cairncross resigning his post (or being fired, depending who you ask).

But Cairncross’ departure is unlikely to change things in the near future – we an expect more tech outages and cyber attacks to come.

In fact Jay Clayton, the National Director of Intelligence, has specifically warned that the next two years will see cyber-outages become routine as “companies update their systems” from “decades-old infrastructure”.

And, ominously, speaking at a recent cyber-security conference at Vanderbilt University, retired General Paul Nakasone – former head of the NSA and US Cyber Command – called the past week of cyber attacks and tech outages “the new normal”.

…don’t you just love that phrase?

So, the narrative is set. We are in the midst of a “cyber-pandemic” of tech outages.

But who is to blame?

And what is the real game here?

Last week, US officials were apparently keen to downplay the idea of any of this being due to a single factor. The line was they were all coincidences and there’s no reason to panic.

But, as we noted at the time, the denials were so thin that they basically played like rather clumsy reverse psychology. Because everyone knows a weakly executed refutation –   “honestly, there’s no reason to panic, however suss it looks” is, under certain circumstances, exactly what you’d say to try and make people panic.

But that was last week. This week there’s a new play in progress.

After noteworthy reticence to lay blame at any state actor before, accusations are now flying thick and fast.

The EU is blaming China.

Google is blaming Russians.

The ex-CIA “intelligence experts” are telling the press that Iran was behind the tech outages – even as the Chief of Homeland Security says they weren’t – mere months after claiming Iran was constantly trying to hack the US’s infrastructure.

“We’re totally under constant cyber-attacks, but every outage was just an accident and nothing to do with Iran”, that’s the official position.

Again, it looks like an unsubtle attempt at damning with faint apology.

It is already, rather predictably, becoming de rigueur to blame Israel, and Trump’s pick for the new US Cyber Security chief – Kirsten Davies – is adding fuel to that fire, with her close associations with Israeli tech firms.

In apparently unrelated news, earlier this week, General Sir Rob Magowan of the UK’s Uber Warfare Unit told the press they were conducting offensive cyber ops against Russia, China, Iran and North Korea.

That is very odd thing to say, isn’t it?

The article notes that “It is very rare for an official to talk publicly about the UK’s covert offensive cyber missions”.

Which is true. I mean you can guess it’s generally considered poor spycraft to announce your “covert missions” – cyber or otherwise – to the international press corps.

…unless of course you’re just another larper larping away on a TV screen to make an increasingly benumbed and bewildered audience  believe you’re engaged in a cyber war, and to begin to associate the deluge of “tech outages” with potential ‘acts of war’.

Is the age of staged warfare to further shared goals expanding into the digital sphere?

The story being constructed seems fairly clear –

We’re being telegraphed the idea we’re in a barely-camouflaged “covert” cyber war with murky enemies of the west. And we’re supposed to divine our “leaders” don’t want us to know about this war – even though they keep making it painfully obvious.

And – of course – just as the physical wars in Iran and Ukraine drove price increases and caused shortages of physical goods, food and energy – this ‘digital war’ is going to disrupt the digital supply chain – meaning tech outages etc.

That’s the “new normal” they’re talking about.

That’s the geopolitics of it all – a story designed to justify declining standards of living.

Which is pretty much what everything boils down to in the end, these days.

If it means anything at all and isn’t just noise for the sake of itself – it means ‘get used to having less and not being especially happy’.

But the true appointed villain of this story – the ultimate perp we are supposed to be shaking our fists at – is not Donald Trump or Israel or Vladimir Putin or Iran –

It is AI.

Not necessarily “rogue” AI, but AI agents being deployed by state or non-state actors.

That’s the constant media refrain.

CrowdStrike is buying ZScaler for $44 million, why? Because “AI is supercharging cyberattacks”.

Google is warning AI is able to make cyberattacks “fully autonomous”. The EU may have blamed China for their hack, but they also made sure to mention it was “AI powered”.

The New York Times reports:

Tech Outages Are Only the Beginning. A.I. Will Bring More Disruptions.

The New York Post is terrified of the “new Chinese AI hacking tool” which allows “anyone with an iPhone to unleash havoc”.

The FBI is “warning” that hackers with AI tools can breach systems in under three hours, with what WIRED calls a “point and shoot” AI hacking tool.

The FT tells us “the AI cyber-threat is already here”, and that firms need to “tighten cyber defences as AI exposes vulnerabilities”.

The Guardian is asking “How freaked out should we be?” in a long article that interviews cyber-security experts who question the “official story” of the tech outages, and blames them all on AI.

As we predicted in our previous article on this, the phrase “digital fragility” is already doing the rounds.

See this piece from Forbes, which notes:

the abrupt fragility of society’s digital infrastructure

It will likely continue to spread, in those words or ones very like them.

That’s the narrative: “Our digital infrastructure is fragile and AI is making cyberattacks – from anarchic digital terrorists or state actors – both easier and more destructive.”

It does get very dull reducing everything down to this dynamic – but we have our problem, we are in the midst of a reaction, and we all know what comes next.

Hint: It starts with “S” and ends with “olution”.

So, what are we going to be told we have to ban, surveil tax or regulate to make this “problem” go away?

Let’s see if we can find some clues…

Writing in the Washington Post, Fareed Zakaria headlines “What grounded planes and downed banking systems say about the AI age”, and his proposed solution is [emphasis added]:

a new digital architecture for the age of AI. The older models of building digital walls are not enough. We must plan for a successful attack. The focus should be on protecting data and restoring functions fast. That means redundancy, segmented or isolated networks, and backups. This is an area where the private sector cannot act alone. An attack on one company or water system can easily spread throughout the country.

This language is edging close to our “worst case scenario” prediction about digital partitions, isn’t it?

Last month, Governor Kathy Hochul of New York signed a new law which age-gates access to AI chatbots. That’s the first law of its type I’m aware of, but we can probably expect them to spread – just as the “social media ban” did.

These morsels gives us a little taste of potential “solutions” to the AI “problem” coming down the line.

The question is if they feel they’ve done enough damage to justify their planned legislation yet, or if we can expect some kind of digital 9/11 first.

articles.title: Keenadu malware found on more than 220,000 Android devices
articles.content:
Kaspersky detected an increase in Android devices with preinstalled malware this year, with the backdoor Keenadu found on more than 220,000 devices between January and October.

Kaspersky researchers report that several large organizations found Keenadu or another backdoor, Triada, on brand-new Android devices after installing the company’s security software.

The cases involved company-owned devices, which organizations often buy in bulk and configure centrally. Malicious code can enter the software supply chain through a firmware contractor or a compromised component that a manufacturer incorporates into its own software.

Two backdoors account for most detections

Kaspersky detected more than 2.5 times as many devices carrying malware in their firmware or system apps in October 2026 as it did in November 2025. Triada and Keenadu accounted for 88% of devices flagged for preinstalled malware from January through October 2026. The company detected Keenadu on more than 220,000 devices in that period across its broader telemetry.

Both backdoors can load additional code and run it inside other apps, including those installed after purchase. Known Triada modules can intercept calls and text messages, steal messaging and social media credentials, or divert cryptocurrency payments. Another module can turn the device into a proxy that relays someone else’s internet traffic.

Keenadu has mostly been observed generating fake ad clicks. Their operators’ servers told the versions Kaspersky analyzed to wait about two and a half months before activating. The researchers suspect the delay helps the malware escape notice while owners set up their devices and install the apps they use every day.

Earlier research also found Keenadu arriving through over-the-air firmware updates on some devices, leaving them open to infection after deployment.

What to do if your device is infected

A factory reset wipes your apps and personal data, but malware built into the device’s system software can survive it.

Kaspersky recommends running a security app to scan your devices, noting that such tools can flag the infection even when they can’t remove it.

If a scan flags preinstalled malware on a new phone or tablet, stop using it and contact the retailer to request a return or refund. If you’ve already signed in, use another device you trust to change the passwords for those accounts, starting with your email.

articles.title: Check Point security management servers hit in global cyberattack campaign
articles.content:
GreyNoise observed 24 compromised Check Point security management servers across 22 organizations in 17 countries, with attackers using 99 IP addresses for scanning and exploitation.

An active intrusion campaign targeting Check Point security management servers has been uncovered, with confirmed attack activity observed between October 17 and November 2, 2026, impacting 22 organizations globally.

Tracked by cybersecurity firm GreyNoise as GreyNoise Threat 13 (GT13), the campaign does not appear to be focused on a single region or industry. Impacted organizations span assets across the US, the UK, Ireland, France, the Netherlands, Greece, Germany, Austria, Bulgaria, Poland, India, Thailand, Vietnam, South Korea, Hong Kong, China, and Australia, across sectors including financial services, energy, government, transportation, mining, engineering, and manufacturing.

“The activity reported by the GreyNoise article involves CVE-2026-16232, a previously disclosed vulnerability with patches already available, and does not represent a new vulnerability or exploitation technique,” a Check Point spokesperson said. “Our priority remains ensuring customers apply the available updates and follow Check Point’s published hardening guidance to restrict management access and identify suspicious activity. The most important action is to install the available updates for CVE-2026-16232. Check Point has already released fixes and detailed mitigation and investigation guidance in its SecureKnowledge advisory.”

GreyNoise has not attributed GT13 to any known or publicly tracked threat group.

“An intrusion into a Check Point security management server is particularly serious because it is not just another server in the enterprise network. It effectively acts as the central control point for managing an organisation’s firewall infrastructure and security policies, with highly privileged access,” said Devroop Dhar, co-founder and MD at Primus Partners. He said that depending on the deployment and the level of access obtained, the consequences could extend well beyond the security infrastructure itself, potentially exposing sensitive data and critical business applications and disrupting enterprise operations.

Building the relay infrastructure

The threat actor operated across 99 IP addresses, primarily routed outbound through ExpressVPN or compromised Check Point devices, generating more than 1,400 network sessions, over 800 command-line artifacts, and over 1,200 created, uploaded, or downloaded files.

GreyNoise first observed the actor scanning and exploiting a Rejetto HFS server on October 2, 2026. Each POST to the HFS loginSrp1 endpoint returned a new signed session cookie containing a “sid” value drawn from JavaScript’s Math.random() function.

Through conducting several logins in succession, the actor collected enough output to reconstruct the internal state of the V8 PRNG algorithm and thus recover an HFS session cookie signing key, then forge a signed admin session cookie. This allowed the attacker to log in as admin without a password.

A few minutes later, GreyNoise observed that admin requests with forged session cookies were used to gain control of the server. This led GreyNoise to believe that exploitation was indeed CVE-2026-61500 for session forgery, which was not patched on this server. The forged cookie contained “allow_session_ip_change:true”, allowing forged cookies to work from any IP address.

On October 5, the actor used this same flow to gain access to install HFS middleware hooks that would issue commands to the compromised server, the research said. This allowed the attacker to append an SSH key to /root/.ssh/authorized_keys. Three days later, on October 8, the threat actor automation check in to the compromised server using the HFS command hook for “uname -a; df -h / | tail -1; whoami”.

Instead of using SSH access right away, on October 19, the actor’s automated pipeline reused the HFS exploitation route to forge new session cookies and leverage the HFS server_code feature to attempt to download and install additional malware on the server. GreyNoise noted that it believes the idea was to use the compromised server as a relay or “hop” for further intrusion operations.

As the malware download failed, the threat actor returned with a direct SSH connection to continue setting up their relay the next day.

On October 20, the threat actor created a script (/root/exfil/srv_post2_<redacted>.py) for setting up an unauthenticated HTTP server on the hop, which they used to upload files. The first exfiltrated .tgz file contained results from a scan of network routes from a compromised Check Point security management server, demonstrating that the actor already had access to targeted victim assets. The actor continued to set up their environment, uploaded and installed open-source tools like Nmap and Chisel, and then set up a Chisel server as a reverse proxy.

Targeted intrusion

Once the compromised server was established as a relay, the actor used it to manage interactions with previously compromised Check Point devices, actively deepening their intrusion against Victim A while conducting bulk actions across 21 other victim organizations. Across the campaign, the operator relied on at least 30 Python scripts, including helpers, launchers, vulnerability probes, and exploit runners.

Between October 20 and 26, the attacker had a compromised Victim A asset download and run Chisel in client mode, allowing them to further scan and interact with Victim A’s environment. Over the Chisel tunnel, and by using a script for CVE-2026-16232, the actor launched over 100 management tasks on multiple Check Point management servers. This included copying the firewall database and the Internal CA, minting a new certificate (pivot.p12), and unloading security policies (which would disable the firewall). Further, the actor probed Citrix NetScaler, Ivanti Connect Secure, VMware vCenter, Microsoft Exchange, Oracle TNS assets and several domain controllers.

Between October 20 and 21, the attacker focused on Victim A, first using exploit.py (CVE-2026-16232) against one Check Point server before scanning a second with spray_portal.py. When that second device failed to report back to the relay box, the actor created pull_<redacted_id>.py to steal credentials, internal CA files, and firewall configurations through the first compromised server.

The attacker then expanded inside Victim A’s network, running broad port scans with curl, telnet, nmap, and a domain controller probe, followed by targeted exploits against internal Microsoft Netlogon, Citrix NetScaler, Ivanti Connect Secure, Microsoft Exchange, and VMware vCenter servers. They wrapped up this phase by running comb.py,ssh_comb.py, and ssh_spray.py populated with victim-themed usernames and passwords.

On October 26, the operation shifted to bulk targeting. The actor issued a bulk certificate management task to 24 compromised Check Point Security Manager servers, including those belonging to Victim A and 21 other victim assets. Results were shipped in a text file to the hop server that contained an incrementing IP order to run the commands on the compromised Check Point servers and deliver them via SCP to this exfil folder. Although the task failed on every device, the error logs sent back to the hop server exposed victim IP addresses and revealed an /etc/ld.so.preload reference to /usr/lib/.libproc.so, pointing to a likely implant before activity paused until November 2.

GreyNoise suspects the GT13 actor has a mature AI-enabled offensive apparatus including separate agentic harnesses and systems weaponizing vulnerabilities, scanning for vulnerable assets, and automatically exploiting.

Securing the management plane

Although GreyNoise’s direct visibility into the campaign paused around November 2, 2026, security leaders must still verify whether their environments have been quietly infiltrated.

With attackers planting backdoors on breached Check Point servers, CISOs must audit their environments for signs of quiet compromise.

To establish whether Check Point infrastructure has been compromised, CISOs and security teams should examine administrative login records for unusual access patterns, including unfamiliar IP addresses, unexpected login times, and unauthorised access added Dhar. They should also look for changes to firewall policies, access-control rules, and configuration files, and thoroughly review system logs, audit trails, and command execution history for suspicious activity.

Dhar noted that once there are indications of a compromise, the immediate priority should be to prevent further access and contain the damage. Security teams should restrict access to the management server to authorised administrative systems and isolate confirmed compromised systems while preserving forensic evidence. Unauthorised accounts should be disabled, suspicious SSH keys and access tokens revoked, and identified malicious IP addresses and domains blocked.

articles.title: Christian Lawyer Challenges Pakistan’s Blasphemy Laws After Death Sentence
articles.content:
by Stefan J. Bos, Worthy News Chief International Correspondent

RAWALPINDI, PAKISTAN (Worthy News) – A Pakistani Christian lawyer has urged Parliament and the judiciary to examine whether the country’s blasphemy laws treat religious communities equally after an anti-terrorism court sentenced a man to death for social media remarks deemed insulting to Islam.

Judge Amjad Ali Shah ruled on November 20 that Muhammad Ibtisam Mustafa was to be executed by hanging over posts on the platform Facebook.

The court, based in Rawalpindi, next to Pakistan’s capital, Islamabad, also imposed life imprisonment for “desecrating” the Quran, which Muslims regard as sacred.

Mustafa received additional prison terms and fines, according to a copy of the court’s warrant provided to Worthy News by lawyer Sardar Mushtaq Gill.

APPEAL DEADLINE

The warrant says Mustafa was informed that he had 15 days from sentencing to appeal to the Lahore High Court. It was unclear whether he had appealed or planned to do so. Pakistani media reports did not quote him or his lawyer in response to the verdict.

The death sentence requires High Court confirmation before it can be carried out.

Pakistan’s newspaper The Express Tribune reported that a higher court in Rawalpindi had previously overturned Mustafa’s sentences three times and ordered the trial court to reconsider the case.

Gill, founder and international advocacy director of the rights group LEAD Ministries, said the complainant’s account also referred to alleged offenses involving Christianity and Hinduism. “The judiciary cannot establish equal religious protection merely by mentioning Christianity and Hinduism in a judgment,” he wrote in a statement sent to Worthy News.

UNEQUAL PENALTIES

The warrant lists four counts under Section 295-A of Pakistan’s Penal Code without specifying which religious beliefs were at issue in each count. Pakistan’s Dawn newspaper reported that an earlier ruling in 2021 convicted Mustafa under the same provision for deliberately insulting Christian beliefs concerning Jesus Christ.

Section 295-A applies to deliberate and malicious insults intended to outrage the religious feelings of any group of Pakistani citizens and carries up to 10 years in prison. Section 295-B prescribes life imprisonment for deliberately desecrating the Quran, while Section 295-C carries a mandatory death sentence for defiling the name of Islam’s Prophet Muhammad. The Penal Code has no equivalent provisions specifically protecting the Bible or Jesus Christ.

Gill urged Pakistan’s chief justice and lawmakers to examine how authorities handle complaints from Christians and other minorities, citing constitutional guarantees of religious freedom and equality before the law.

“Religious equality does not mean multiplying harsh punishments; it means protecting everyone’s religious freedom, human dignity, freedom of expression and right to justice without discrimination,” he stressed.

CHRISTIANS IN PAKISTAN

Christian advocacy group Open Doors ranks Pakistan eighth on its 2026 World Watch List of 50 countries where Christians face the most severe persecution.

“Increasingly, Pakistan’s notorious blasphemy laws are used to intimidate Christians and other religious minorities,” the group says in its country profile.

Pakistan’s 2023 census counted about 3.3 million Christians, or 1.4 percent of the Muslim-majority nation’s roughly 241 million residents.

In its 2026 country profile, Open Doors estimates that Christians make up 1.9 percent of Pakistan’s population, or about 4.8 million people.

The post Christian Lawyer Challenges Pakistan’s Blasphemy Laws After Death Sentence appeared first on Worthy Christian News.

articles.title: Remus Stealer’s claimed Gmail zero-day is a malicious Chrome extension
articles.content:
Remus Stealer’s advertised Gmail “zero-day” is a malicious Chrome extension disguised as Google Sheets.

The extension can resume stealing emails after a password reset if the victim signs back in using the infected browser.

GenDigital researchers traced the feature to a module that some versions of Remus download after the malware starts running. The researchers initially found no mailbox interception code in the main stealer binary and later recovered the separate module.

As we previously reported, Remus operators began promoting the feature on November 8, claiming that access would survive password changes and session revocation. Hudson Rock spoke with the developer and a customer who endorsed the feature, but could not independently confirm how it worked. Remus is sold as a service that collects passwords and other sensitive data from infected computers. Its operators advertised Gmail interception as part of a $1,000-a-month Enterprise tier.

A fake Google Sheets extension

On an infected Windows computer, the module alters Chrome’s profile settings to install the extension and switch on Developer Mode. It labels the extension “Google Sheets” and copies the description of Google’s legitimate Docs Offline extension. GenDigital found that the module targets Chrome and that the fake Sheets entry carries an icon identifying it as an unpacked extension.

Once installed, the extension checks for unread Gmail messages every minute across up to 10 accounts signed in to the same browser profile. It uses those active sessions to retrieve message bodies and sends the text, subject, sender, and recipient account address to an attacker-controlled server. GenDigital found that the extension records attachment names while processing messages but sends neither the names nor the files.

That lets attackers capture verification codes and password-reset links as they arrive, along with private correspondence and work emails. Anyone who uses the same Chrome profile for personal and work Gmail could expose both accounts.

Signing back in restores access

Signing out or revoking the Gmail session cuts off the extension’s access. The extension stays installed on the computer, however, and can start reading new messages as soon as the victim signs back in. That distinction explains how email theft could resume after an account reset.

If you suspect a Remus infection, change your Google password and revoke affected sessions from a clean device. Before signing back in on the affected computer, scan it for malware and check each Chrome profile separately at 

chrome://extensions
for an unfamiliar Google Sheets entry or other unexpected extensions. Google also recommends reviewing connected devices and checking for unfamiliar Gmail forwarding rules and filters as part of its account recovery guidance.

articles.title: Is “Epstein Didn’t Kill Himself” going mainstream?
articles.content:
Is “Epstein Didn’t Kill Himself” going mainstream?

When it comes to anti-establishment catchphrases, “Epstein Didn’t Kill Himself” is probably second only to “Jet Fuel Doesn’t Melt Steel Beams” in terms of pop culture footprint.

The two phrases are twinned in that way, punchlines removed from the jokes. Words memed into quasi-meaninglessness by over repetition.

But the Epstein line appears  – suddenly – to be doing something jet fuel never could – getting serious mainstream consideration and  air time.

Forensic pathologist Dr Michael Freeman has come forward asserting he disagrees with the official autopsy findings of suicide, and that his interpretation is that evidence points far more directly at homicide.

Dr Freeman is editor-in-chief of the Journal of Forensic and Legal Medicine and, according to CBS, was granted access to the confidential medical and police files by Jeffrey Epstein’s brother.

Amazingly, his revelations have been covered by pretty much every major network…

On the 16th he was on the BBC’s Newsnight:

“So you are saying that Epstein was killed by another person?”

Michael Freeman, a prominent expert in forensic medicine, speaks to #Newsnight about his claims that Jeffrey Epstein’s death was a “result of a homicide”.

Warning: Distressing details of death and injury and discussion of suicide

— BBC Newsnight (@BBCNewsnight) November 16, 2026

Note the BBC tells us Freeman is a “prominent expert”, NOT a “crazy conspiracy theorist”.

Interesting, no?

And again, in the BBC’s main write up he’s presented as a “forensic expert”,

We’re being telegraphed that Freeman is a person we ought to listen to.

CBS, the New York Post, the New York Times and Channel 4 in the UK have all run with the same line on this story, and only CNN have put even a hint of reservation in their headline:

Forensic expert says Epstein was likely killed, but NYC medical examiner stands by suicide ruling

Prominent author and podcaster Sam Harris released a video three days ago titled “Why I’m Reconsidering Jeffrey Epstein’s Death”.

TMZ have gone with it in their uniquely TMZ-ish style:

JEFFREY EPSTEIN’S DEATH FORENSIC EXPERTS REVEAL NEW THEORY…This Was No Suicide!!!

Three exclamation points. Classy stuff.

So – why exactly is this happening?

I trust we are all sufficiently awake and aware that we can immediately rule out any fanciful notions these outlets are saying this stuff “because it’s true”.

I mean, that Epstein didn’t kill himself almost certainly IS true – one way or another – but it was just as true 7 long years ago when these outfits were all insisting he simply offed himself.

These state sponsored propaganda machines don’t say things because they’re true.

They don’t care or even acquaint themselves with what’s true. It’s not their brief.

And that doesn’t change because something is obviously super duper true.

It simply does not matter how true a thing is – the propaganda machine will simply ignore it, step over it, walk right past it.

If it isn’t briefed to talk about something,  it won’t. Even if it happens to be the biggest most blatant truth in the universe.

I mean, just look around you. Whistleblowers, experts and journalists have been questioning the “official versions” of newsworthy deaths from JFK to George Floyd and producing solid evidence for doing so – but if those questions don’t serve an agenda they generally don’t get on the news.

And they certainly don’t get on the news without the usual eye-rolling “this guy’s a crazy conspiracy theorist, here’s an article about how anyone who agrees with him is ugly and has no friends” rider.

So, don’t fall for the lame “oh FINALLY the mainstream are seeing the light” line.

No. They haven’t. They won’t. They can’t. They are just using a little bit of potential truth to sell you another mountain of lies and distortion.

Oh, and Speaking of George Floyd…

A leading pathologist says there was “zero per cent chance” that convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein died by suicide.

Professor Michael Freeman is a cause of death specialist, who was an expert witness in the George Floyd case.

After reviewing the New York medical examiner’s file provided to him by Epstein’s family, he said the most likely cause was an assault followed by strangulation from behind.

— Channel 4 News (@Channel4News) November 17, 2026

It just so happens Dr Freeman was an “expert witness” in the George Floyd case, who testified to its being a homicide, despite the original autopsy finding it to be a drug overdose.

And again, note he’s presented to us as an “expert witness” a “leading pathologist” and a “cause of death specialist”, he is NOT tagged as a “rogue pathologist”, “conspiracy theorist” or “controversial figure”.

So what do we have here?

We have a “leading pathologist”, with a history of making politically convenient statements that serve the agenda (eg. George Floyd), suddenly “revealing” that Epstein didn’t kill himself, and being given a platform to do so in a lot of mainstream media.

If you’re not up to speed yet – what you’re looking at here is narrative creation to serve an agenda.

What will the narrative/agenda turn out to be?

Is there going to be a witch hunt to “identify” Epstein’s likely “murderer(s)”? Will there be lurid allegations and crazy assumptions circulating about all the usual hate figures?

Let’s wait to see.

It should also be noted this bullhorned “revelation” is accompanied by a few other Epstein-adjacent stories.

Earlier this month, the US House Oversight Committee published their 137-page report on the “mishandling” of the Epstein case. The New York Times published a video about what comes next in that process just four days ago.

Sky News reports that the police are “examining claims” that Epstein was involved in trafficking women to the Balmoral estate owned by the Royal Family.

Forbes is headlining “Deutsche Bank Leak Reveals $582 Million In Suspicious Epstein Payments”

And Reuters have published a special report – “Why Epstein Loved Russia” – which they rather comically volunteer…

found no evidence Jeffrey Epstein worked for Russian intelligence, acted for the Russian government or met Vladimir Putin.

These are just in the last couple of days.

So maybe we are also going to get a fresh wave of “friend of Epstein” type hysteria – possibly aimed at bringing down one or two prominent-yet-disposable public figures.

With the Democrats just “winning” the mid-terms, the odds are it will be a Republican, or Republican-aligned figure…or maybe an Israeli. Or maybe a mixed bag of entities they want to discredit or just retire from public life.

For a little confirmation that this aspect might be in the offing, check out this Reuters piece on Robert Garcia, expected to become the next chair of the oversight committee…

Representative Robert Garcia, the likely next House oversight committee chair, sent letters on ​Wednesday to 12 of President Donald Trump’s top allies, former aides and family members, signaling planned investigations into alleged Trump family corruption, ‌the Jeffrey Epstein files and the administration’s immigration crackdown.

Garcia is among the newly empowered Democrats who swept to power in this month’s midterm elections and who plan to use that oversight ability to, as Garcia said in a statement, “put an end to this Administration’s self-dealing, misconduct and abuse.”

articles.title: ASUS fixes critical remote command execution flaw in GPU Tweak III
articles.content:
ASUS has released a security update for its GPU Tweak III utility to address a critical vulnerability that allows remote attackers to execute arbitrary operating system commands on affected computers.

The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-114203, carries a CVSS v4.0 severity score of 9.3 out of 10 and was disclosed by the Taiwanese hardware manufacturer on November 24, 2026.

GPU Tweak III is a Windows-based graphics card management and overclocking utility that lets gamers and enthusiasts adjust clock speeds, voltages, and fan curves; monitor hardware performance; and create custom performance profiles.

The utility supports both NVIDIA and AMD graphics cards, including those from manufacturers other than ASUS, extending the potential impact of the vulnerability beyond the company’s own hardware customers.

According to the CVE record, the security issue is classified as an operating system command injection vulnerability.

The vulnerability affects GPU Tweak III versions 1.6.9.4 through 2.2.1.1, inclusive.

Successful exploitation does not require authentication, elevated privileges, or interaction from the victim. The resulting unauthorized command execution could expose affected computers to data theft, unauthorized system modifications, and disruption of normal operations.

However, ASUS has not clarified whether vulnerable installations are accessible from the internet under default configurations or whether exploitation requires access to the victim’s local network. The computer software and hardware manufacturer has also not provided information about the privileges under which injected commands would execute.

The security bulletin does not mention any observed attempts to exploit the flaw in attacks.

ASUS is urging GPU Tweak III users to immediately download and install the latest available software release from its official support website.

Users who no longer rely on GPU Tweak III for graphics card management should consider uninstalling the utility altogether to reduce their system’s attack surface.

articles.title: Lawyers Urge Pakistan To Free Christian Sentenced To Death For Blasphemy
articles.content:
by Stefan J. Bos, Worthy News Chief International Correspondent

LAHORE, PAKISTAN (Worthy News) – A Christian legal advocacy group has urged Pakistan to free Shahzad Masih, a Pakistani Christian arrested at age 16 and later sentenced to death for blasphemy after allegedly repeating another person’s remarks about Islam’s Prophet Muhammad.

Masih has spent more than nine years in prison. His appeal remains pending before the Lahore High Court despite repeated requests for a hearing, the American Center for Law and Justice (ACLJ) said. Its Pakistani affiliate, the Organization for Legal Aid, represents him.

Masih was working at a hospital in Punjab Province when a coworker asked him about his religious beliefs in July 2017, according to the ACLJ. His lawyers say he repeated remarks he attributed to a family acquaintance. A trial court sentenced him to death by hanging on November 22, 2022.

“We urge Pakistani authorities to uphold fundamental human rights, overturn this unjust conviction, and bring Shahzad Masih home to his family,” said CeCe Heil, the ACLJ’s senior counsel and international legal director.

UN URGES MASIH’S RELEASE

The United Nations Working Group on Arbitrary Detention found in an opinion published in February 2024 that Masih’s imprisonment was arbitrary and that his fair-trial rights had been violated. It called for his immediate release, compensation and an independent investigation. The working group said Pakistan’s government had not replied to its request for information.

Masih was convicted under Section 295-C of Pakistan’s Penal Code, which carries the death penalty for derogatory remarks about Muhammad. Pakistan has never carried out a state execution for blasphemy. The Pakistani Center for Research and Security Studies documented 104 extrajudicial killings following blasphemy accusations between 1948 and May 2024, according to a British Home Office briefing.

Two other Christians were acquitted in Lahore this year, Christian Daily International reported. A court cleared Nadeem Masih, a blind Catholic, in June after 10 months in prison, citing insufficient evidence.

In July, a court acquitted Dennis Albert after he spent more than two years in prison on an accusation of desecrating pages of the Quran. His lawyer said the court found flaws in the police investigation and inconsistencies in the prosecution’s evidence.

CHRISTIAN PERSECUTION IN PAKISTAN

In a separate case, Amir Peter, a Christian with advanced dementia, died in custody in July after nearly a year awaiting trial on a blasphemy charge. The advocacy group representing him said he had received inadequate medical care.

Advocacy group Open Doors ranks Muslim-majority Pakistan eighth on its 2026 World Watch List of the 50 countries where Christians reportedly face the most severe persecution.

Open Doors says blasphemy accusations in Muslim-majority Pakistan can spark mob violence against the accused, their families and the wider Christian community.

The group estimates that about 4.8 million Christians live in Pakistan, making up roughly 1.9 percent of its population of about 250 million.

The post Lawyers Urge Pakistan To Free Christian Sentenced To Death For Blasphemy appeared first on Worthy Christian News.

articles.title: Something Went Terribly Wrong In This NIH-Funded Bat Virus Experiment
articles.content:
This post was republished with permission from Zero Hedge

The National Institutes of Health paid for a Hendra virus experiment on bats in Australia that the lab’s own ethics committee shut down in 2023, after staff had to kill all eight bats in a room because they could not raise it to the highest biocontainment level once one bat tested positive, according to federal records obtained by PETA and reviewed by Fox News Digital.

Hendra is a lethal virus carried by flying foxes. The study, titled “Shining a light on bat cellular immunity following virus infection,” ran at the Australian Centre for Disease Preparedness, the high-containment lab run by Australia’s national science agency, CSIRO. The NIH grant behind it (R21AI169481) ran from 2022 to 2024 and totaled about $146,098, with Monash University as a collaborator.

The records cite a shortage of staff trained to handle animals at the required biocontainment level, no adequate contingency plan, unclear protocols and flying foxes kept confined for long stretches without proper enrichment. When one flying fox tested positive, the eight bats housed with it were killed because the room could not be brought up to Biosafety Level 4 (BSL-4). Then a ninth bat, one kept apart in a BSL-4 room, turned up positive too and was put down.

The lead investigator told the NIH about the infections in May 2023, and the ethics committee suspended the study weeks later. Word of the suspension didn’t reach the NIH’s Office of Laboratory Animal Welfare (OLAW), even in preliminary form, until April 2024, more than 10 months after the study was halted, the records show.

A system run on self-reporting

PETA says it went through 124 federal files obtained under the Freedom of Information Act. Of 70 annual reports filed between 2023 and 2025 by foreign labs doing NIH-backed animal research, 67 reported zero violations.

The NIH’s inspections of those labs are virtual. Site visits were announced months ahead: Newcastle University in the UK, which runs NIH-funded brain and stroke research on monkeys, got notice in May 2025 of a virtual visit that took place in December. The notification letters set out planning sessions, document reviews and camera tours in which the foreign lab’s own staff controlled what federal monitors could see on screen. There were no unannounced walk-throughs, no rooms picked at random, no real-time record checks and no confidential staff interviews, the records show.

The same 2025 review ordered Newcastle to reevaluate its protective equipment standards, its tuberculosis screening and its emergency procedures for testing staff potentially exposed to Herpes B, a monkey virus that can kill humans.

The NIH had pledged “enhanced oversight” of foreign labs after a run of scandals, including Colombia’s Caucaseco Scientific Research Center, where PETA documented monkeys kept in squalor. The NIH cut off Caucaseco and an affiliated malaria vaccine center in July 2023, after the two had collectively received $17 million in NIH funding.

Labs with no license at all

Some of the money went to labs that never held the basic NIH paperwork. The agency awarded the University of Sydney a $13 million contract in 2022 for tuberculosis vaccine adjuvant work, but the animal testing was farmed out to Australia’s Centenary Institute, which lacked the NIH Foreign Animal Welfare Assurance every foreign lab needs. The NIH didn’t notice for years, until the university asked about the death of an experimental mouse in 2025.

The NIH also told PETA it could find “no records of an assurance” for several foreign outfits running US-funded animal studies, among them Australian biotech Kinoxis Therapeutics, which ran opioid withdrawal experiments on 80 dogs, 314 rats and 1,485 mice under a grant active through May 2026. The records show the same gap for grants involving animal testing in Canada, Kenya and Israel.

The NIH also paid for several years of Chagas disease research on mice at Argentina’s Research Center in Clinical Biochemistry and Immunology. A 2026 preprint co-authored by its lead researcher described mice with continuous whole-body tremors and hind-limb paralysis, conditions that call for euthanasia under the approved protocol. Instead, untreated animals died over as long as 120 days, and the lab admitted it keeps no animal monitoring or veterinary records.

Cut it off

PETA sent a complaint on Monday to NIH Director Jay Bhattacharya demanding that the agency stop funding all animal experiments outside the US. The letter, from PETA congressional liaison Magnolia Martínez, calls the foreign monitoring regime fundamentally broken and argues that an Animal Welfare Assurance is a box-ticking requirement that guarantees neither animal welfare nor results that apply to humans.

Bhattacharya has said the NIH now demands direct auditing relationships with foreign institutions on the work it funds, so that it “can shut off money” to one that isn’t cooperating, a lesson he tied to the Wuhan Institute of Virology, whose lab notebooks were never obtained. Trump’s executive order last year banned federal funding for dangerous gain-of-function research in countries like China and Iran and in nations without adequate research oversight.

In Congress, the bipartisan Cease Animal Research Grants Overseas (CARGO) Act, S. 1802 in the Senate, would bar the NIH from funding live-animal research outside the US. Sen. Rick Scott (R-Fla.), who introduced it with Sen. Cory Booker (D-N.J.) in May 2025, called it “deeply concerning” that taxpayer dollars had funded “harmful and abusive animal experiments.” Reps. Troy Nehls (R-Texas) and Dina Titus (D-Nev.) carry the House version.

Closer to home, the CDC is winding down its own in-house monkey program, after quarantine screening found 69 tuberculosis cases in incoming macaques between 2021 and 2024, according to internal data PETA reviewed.
